sources.title: Bryan Johnson's simplified morning routine: light, hair care, Blueprint stack, exercise, red light, meditation
sources.summary: Bryan walks through his streamlined morning: sleep data, light and temperature checks, hair serums and red light cap, Blueprint longevity mix and nutty pudding, daily workout, 6-minute red light therapy, a high-fiber super veggie breakfast and a time-travel meditation. He stresses lab-testing everything and keeping the routine simple, affordable and consistent.

principles.text: Map your morning into a fixed sequence of steps so it happens automatically every day.

principles.text: Exercise is non-negotiable: do it every single day, no deciding.
principles.quote: now I'm going to work out where it's not a question if I'm going to work out I just do it every single day

principles.text: Don't trust labels; lab-test supplements and foods for contents and heavy metals.
principles.quote: we learned that basically we don't trust anyone the only thing you can trust is data

principles.text: Sleep, exercise and good eating are the foundation that keeps you calm under stress.
principles.quote: because I have my basics of Health and Wellness in place of like good sleep and exercise and eating well I just handle these things with much more calm

principles.text: Start hair care early, in your 20s, since lost hair is hard to recover.

principles.text: Eat a very high-fiber diet, over 30 g a day, about 3x the average American.
principles.quote: my diet is uh has over 30 g a day of fiber so the average American I think get somewhere around 10 so I'm about 3x

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's five pillars of exercise for longevity
sources.summary: Bryan lays out five exercise pillars for longevity: strength training, zone 2 cardio, high-intensity cardio (VO2 max), mobility and balance. He gives weekly targets, his own protocol and the mortality data behind each pillar, and stresses consistency and measurement over finding a perfect routine.

principles.text: Exercise is non-negotiable for longevity; it lowers all-cause mortality by 31%.
principles.quote: if you want to live long, exercise is non-negotiable. In fact, regular exercise can reduce the risk of all-cause mortality by 31%.

principles.text: Train all systems: strength, zone 2, high-intensity cardio, mobility and balance. Don't hyper-focus on one form.
principles.quote: the real question isn't what's the best type of exercise, it's what combination of exercises keeps you alive the longest.

principles.text: Strength train at least 3x/week with compound movements and progressive overload.
principles.quote: Aim for at least three strength-building sessions per week. Focus on compound movements that train the entire body. Push. Pull. Squat.

principles.text: Do about 150 minutes of zone 2 cardio weekly, plus a 10-minute walk after meals for blood sugar.
principles.quote: I personally aim for 150 minutes of zone two cardio per week.

principles.text: VO2 max is a top longevity predictor; do about 75 minutes of high-intensity cardio weekly, e.g. the Norwegian 4x4.
principles.quote: I aim for 75 minutes of high intensity cardio each week.

principles.text: Use a heart rate monitor to stay in the right zones; measurement and data are everything.
principles.quote: As with all things blueprint, measurement and data is everything.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's anti-aging skincare routine: measure, protect, and keep only what moves the data
sources.summary: Bryan tours his Blueprint skin protocol: a minimal morning routine, strict sun avoidance, and a clinic of devices (multispectral imaging, tixel, IPL/BBL, red light). His core rule is that every cream or device must prove itself on measurable markers or it is cut. Creams rarely move the data, while devices do.

principles.text: Every skincare product or device must prove itself on measurable markers or it gets cut from the protocol.
principles.quote: if we don't hit the markers the technology is out

principles.text: Creams don't move the needle on measured skin data; devices like lasers and IPL do.
principles.quote: creams don't move the needle on data

principles.text: Avoid sun damage: stay out of high-UV hours, use sunscreen when outside, and cut UV at home with window tint.
principles.quote: the most effective thing to do is avoid the damage if you're going to be outside wear sunscreen

principles.text: Use clinical-grade multispectral imaging to track UV damage, pores, reds and browns instead of judging by eye.
principles.quote: UV damage which you can't see with your eye it's on a machine using multi-spectral Imaging

principles.text: Keep the daily routine simple: wash, apply a trial cream, then sunscreen.
principles.quote: in summary the routine is very simple I wash with this in the morning I put this cream on

principles.text: Keep red light therapy (3x/week, 12 minutes) on evidence of general benefit even when its effect can't be measured directly.
principles.quote: I do this uh three times a week uh for 12 minutes so it's a total of uh 36 minutes a week

sources.title: Resting heart rate before bed: Bryan Johnson on evening exercise, sleep and the one marker that matters
sources.originalTitle: Evening Exercise, Poor Sleep, and Resting Heart Rate | Bryan Johnson Podcast
sources.summary: Bryan discusses a Whoop study of 4.3M nights showing strenuous exercise within about 4-6 hours of bed hurts sleep. He argues resting heart rate before bed is the single most important biomarker, and lays out a practical protocol to lower it: eat earlier and lighter, screens off, a wind-down routine, no blue light, and consistency.

principles.text: Resting heart rate before bed is the single most important biomarker; it captures food, stress, fitness and habits.
principles.quote: I have been talking about resting heart rate as the single most important biomarker of my entire life as all the efforts we've done basically collapse into this marker.

principles.text: Strenuous exercise too close to bed worsens sleep; do hard training at least 4 hours, ideally 6+, before bed.
principles.quote: strenuous exercise should happen at least four hours before bed, probably closer to six hours before bed.

principles.text: Sleep is the top priority; prioritizing it raises willpower, exercise and good eating.
principles.quote: sleep deserves being the number one spot in everyone's life above family, above work, above everything. It is the fuel source of existence.

principles.text: Eat the last meal early and light; Bryan finishes around noon after testing many meal times.
principles.quote: I have my final meal of the day at around noon. And so, that's roughly 8 and a half hours before my bedtime.

principles.text: Turn screens off 60 minutes before bed and use a wind-down routine, avoiding blue light.
principles.quote: the rule here is screens off 60 minutes before bed.

principles.text: Assume people share most biology; look for the rule first rather than assuming you are the exception.
principles.quote: we have more in common than we do indifferent.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's sleep protocol: resting heart rate before bed and 10 tips for high-quality sleep
sources.originalTitle: My Advanced Guide To Better Sleep | Bryan Johnson Podcast
sources.summary: Bryan treats sleep as a craft to master, anchored on one metric: resting heart rate just before bed. He lays out ten practical rules (early light meal, wind-down, light, consistency, stimulants, temperature, noise, wearable) and says anything that raises pre-bed heart rate degrades sleep.

principles.text: Treat sleep as a craft: be on time to bed like for a meeting, and see yourself as a professional sleeper.
principles.quote: You need to think about sleep as you would anything you take seriously. A a hobby, your job, you know, being a parent, you need to try to perfect the craft.

principles.text: Use resting heart rate before bed as the master metric: what raises it hurts sleep, what lowers it helps.
principles.quote: My sleep depends upon my resting heart rate before bed. And so I've tried to structure my entire life around this idea of things that increase my resting heart rate are bad.

principles.text: Finish eating at least 4 hours before bed; Bryan eats about 8 hours before, and lighter foods help.
principles.quote: you want to have your final meal of the day at least 4 hours before bed. You can experiment with 2, three, four, five, six, seven. I have my last meal of the day around 8 hours or so before my bedtime

principles.text: Do a 30 to 60 minute screen-free wind-down: walk, meditate, breath work, a book in hand.
principles.quote: you need to have a 30 to 60 minute wind down routine every day. Your you can't just finish work and then 30 seconds later you just put your head on the pillow and fall asleep.

principles.text: Get bright light within minutes of waking (Bryan uses a 10,000 lux light at 4:30 a.m.) and keep a consistent bedtime.
principles.quote: I wake up before the sun rises around 4:30 a.m. So, I use a 10,000 lux light in my home.

principles.text: Mind stimulants and blue light: caffeine has a roughly 6-hour half-life, evenings should be red or amber light.
principles.quote: caffeine has roughly a 6 hour half-life. So a cup of coffee at 4 p.m. is a half a cup of coffee in you at 10 p.m. when you're asleep.

sources.title: Don't Die Basics: Sleep First, Willpower, and Cheap Habits Over Expensive Therapies
sources.originalTitle: “These Basic Health Habits Beat Expensive Therapies” - Bryan Johnson (4K)
sources.summary: Bryan explains why sleep is the master lever: nighttime erections as a health biomarker, a pre-bed routine that lowers resting heart rate, and how sleep restores the willpower needed to quit bad habits. He also shares sauna and HBOT results, a no-moderation rule on food, and his plan to reframe death-culture status with Don't Die.

principles.text: Nighttime erections are a representative health biomarker driven by sleep, metabolic, cardiovascular and hormone health; you can't force them.
principles.quote: men and women have arousal cycles every night. Three to five erections every night.

principles.text: Do less: most wellness tactics don't work; the biggest yield is behavior change, like stopping the one bad habit, not compensating with therapies.
principles.quote: Most things in health and wellness and longevity don't work. And so people spend a lot of time doing stuff and I would say save your time and money and don't do a lot of stuff.

principles.text: Lower resting heart rate before bed: final meal 4 hours before, screens off 60 minutes before, amber light, calm wind-down, last caffeine around noon.
principles.quote: You want to lower your resting heart rate before bed? It's the highest value biomarker you can track on a daily basis.

principles.text: Sleep regularity matters most; the body runs on a fixed circadian schedule and you can't make up missed sleep on weekends.
principles.quote: Inconsistent sleep is as bad as little sleep.

principles.text: Prefer habits over pills for sleep; he takes only a tiny 300 mcg melatonin dose to offset pineal calcification.
principles.quote: I do a very tiny dose of melatonin. Uh it's to offset the calcification that happens in my pinal gland.

principles.text: Order of attack: master sleep first, then exercise (about an hour of activity daily), then food; no cheat meals, none is better than some.
principles.quote: Like none is better than some. So there's no moderation.

principles.text: Sleep is the top performance enhancer, and a temperature-controlled mattress meaningfully improves his sleep.

sources.title: How I fixed my terrible sleep: Bryan's 10 habits for perfect sleep
sources.originalTitle: How I Fixed My Terrible Sleep
sources.summary: Bryan lays out ten habits behind eight months of 100% perfect sleep: treat sleep as priority one, wind down, manage light and temperature, keep a fixed bedtime, eat early, skip stimulants, and track data. He backs it with sleep-deprivation research and his own data on meal timing and resting heart rate.

principles.text: Make sleep your number one priority and plan your day around it.
principles.quote: Make sleep your #1 priority. Nothing influences your conscious existence more.

principles.text: Do a 30-60 minute wind-down routine: reading, mindfulness or breathing, soothing music.
principles.quote: Create a 30-60 minute Wind-Down Routine: Set a specific time each evening to start wind down

principles.text: Get outside within 15-30 minutes of waking to anchor your circadian rhythm.
principles.quote: Get outside within the first 15-30 minutes of waking to set your circadian rhythm and boost mood.

principles.text: Dim and warm the lights 1-2 hours before bed, limit screens, and black out the bedroom.
principles.quote: Dim the lights one to two hours before bedtime to create a relaxed atmosphere.

principles.text: Keep the bedroom between 60-67°F and sleep on a consistent schedule, even on weekends.
principles.quote: Keep your bedroom temperature between 60-67°F (15-19°C).

principles.text: Eat the last meal hours before bed; Bryan eats at 11 am, which lowers his resting heart rate and improves sleep.
principles.quote: If I eat later in the day, my resting heart rate will be between 55-58 bpm because my body is still digesting food and it will lessen my sleep quality by ~30%.

sources.title: Lower your heart rate before sleep: Bryan Johnson's #1 health tip and HRBS protocol
sources.originalTitle: How to Lower Your Heart Rate Before Sleep
sources.summary: Bryan argues heart rate before sleep (HRBS) is the single most important health metric and a longevity lever, because it predicts sleep quality. He explains how to measure it, what a good score is, and gives a protocol of food, caffeine, exercise, stress and light habits that lowers it.

principles.text: If you focus on one health thing, lower your heart rate before sleep.
principles.quote: But if you're going to focus on one thing, it would be this: Lower your heart rate before sleep.

principles.text: HRBS is a single-number biomarker of fitness, metabolic health, food habits and stress management.
principles.quote: HRBS is a powerful biomarker of overall health. A single number representing how your whole body is doing.

principles.text: Lower HRBS means faster, deeper sleep, and sleep is the #1 longevity therapy.
principles.quote: This is critical because sleep is the #1 longevity therapy.

principles.text: Measure HRBS lying flat for 60 seconds; use a wearable or count the pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Around 50 bpm is great.
principles.quote: If you don't, count your pulse for 15 seconds and then multiply by 4

principles.text: His HRBS predicts his sleep quality: around 40 bpm gives a perfect night, 57 bpm costs about 30% of sleep quality.
principles.quote: If it's 40 bpm, I am guaranteed a perfect night's sleep. If it's 57 bpm, I'll lose about 30% of my sleep quality.

principles.text: Finish food about 4 hours before bed, avoid heavy meals and alcohol, and end caffeine by 12pm.
principles.quote: Finish all food ~4 hours before bed (earlier the better)

sources.title: How Bryan Johnson achieved a 100% sleep score: six rules for reliably great sleep
sources.summary: Bryan explains how he reached eight months of perfect sleep scores by treating sleep as a top priority. He covers meal timing, light exposure, wind-down routines, consistent bedtimes and managing caffeine.

principles.text: Treat sleep with the same seriousness and devotion as work; build your life around it.
principles.quote: You need to treat sleep with the same level of seriousness and devotion as you do your work. It demands your best performance.

principles.text: Finish your last meal at least two hours before bed, gradually moving it earlier to lower resting heart rate.
principles.quote: If your bedtime is 10 PM, finish eating by 8 PM. Then day by day, move it back by 30 minutes.

principles.text: A lower resting heart rate at bedtime means better sleep.
principles.quote: The lower your resting heart rate, the better your sleep.

principles.text: Avoid blue light an hour or two before bed; use red and amber lights instead.
principles.quote: An hour or two before bed, try to avoid blue light. That means turn off screens, or eliminate blue light from your screens

principles.text: Create a wind-down routine that separates you from work and calms body and mind.
principles.quote: You can't just finish work and put your head on the pillow and expect great sleep. You need to calm your body and mind down.

principles.text: Keep bedtime consistent, within +/- 30 minutes every day, because the body rewards routine.
principles.quote: Go to bed within +/- 30 minutes of your chosen bedtime every single day. Create the habit and stay with the habit.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's exercise protocol: a weekly mix for longevity
sources.originalTitle: Exercise and Fitness Protocol for Longevity
sources.summary: Bryan lays out his weekly exercise framework: consistency over intensity, four categories (strength, zone 2, HIIT, mobility), his weekly targets, a sample 7-day routine, and pre/post-workout nutrition with Blueprint products. He stresses that even 11 minutes a day matters.

principles.text: Small daily exercise habits deliver real longevity benefits; consistency beats occasional all-out efforts.
principles.quote: 11 min of daily exercise is linked to a [23% lower risk](https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/57/15/979) of early death.

principles.text: No single exercise is best; cover four categories each week.
principles.quote: No single exercise is best. A mix is best.

principles.text: Do 2-3 strength sessions weekly with compound movements and progressive overload.
principles.quote: aim for 2-3 strength training sessions a week:** Focus on compound movements, such as squats, deadlifts, and lunges

principles.text: HIIT gives the best return on time, and cardiorespiratory fitness strongly predicts lifespan.
principles.quote: HIIT is the best ROI for your time:

principles.text: Avoid high-intensity exercise within 4 hours of bed to protect sleep and recovery.
principles.quote: avoid high-intensity exercise 4 hours before bed:** Research shows it can reduce sleep quality and recovery.

principles.text: His weekly targets: 150+ min zone 2, 75+ min high-intensity, daily mobility/balance work.
principles.quote: at least 150 min of zone 2 cardio a week

sources.title: Blueprint Recipes: the 14 plant-based meals Bryan Johnson eats

principles.text: Bryan treats eating as one of life's greatest joys, so his meals are enjoyable, not just functional.
principles.quote: Here’s a list of the recipes I’ve been eating lately. One of life’s greatest joys for me.

sources.title: How Bryan Johnson makes his daily anti-aging "Super Veggie" lunch

sources.summary: Bryan shares the exact recipe and cooking method for Super Veggie, the meal he eats every day. It combines black lentils, cruciferous vegetables, mushrooms and spices, cooked at low temperature with high humidity and acidity to limit AGEs and ALEs.

principles.text: Cook with low temperature, high humidity, high acidity and high antioxidants to minimize AGEs and ALEs.

principles.quote: When starting, sometimes there is a period of adaptation and some want to play with the recipe and texture.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's haircare protocol: nutrition, peptides, laser cap and minoxidil
sources.summary: Bryan lays out the five-part routine he credits for having better hair at 49 than 29, with about 70% of his gray gone. It covers nutrition, Blueprint peptide shampoo and serum, a daily laser cap, oral minoxidil and topical minoxidil, plus advice to start before thinning is visible.

principles.text: Good hair starts with whole-food nutrition: enough protein, omega-3 and key vitamins and minerals.
principles.quote: Your body needs good food to make good hair.

principles.text: Avoid processed junk and added sugar; hair needs iron, selenium, biotin, zinc, and vitamins C, D, E.
principles.quote: In general, eat whole foods and avoid processed junk and added sugar.

principles.text: Scalp routine: peptide shampoo left on for 2 min, then peptide serum massaged in with a silicone scrubber for blood flow.
principles.quote: I apply [Peptide Hair Serum](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/hair-peptide-serum) and massage it into my scalp with a silicone scrubber for 1–2 min to stimulate blood flow.

principles.text: Wear a low-level laser cap for 6 minutes a day to support regrowth.
principles.quote: I wear the [302 Laser Cap](https://blueprint.bryanjohnson.com/products/laser-cap) for 6 min a day.

principles.text: Oral minoxidil titrated up from 2.5 mg to 3.75 mg while watching for side effects, plus 1 mL of 5% topical nightly.
principles.quote: I started with 2.5 mg and evaluated for side effects. I now take 3.75 mg a day.

principles.text: Start a hair protocol before thinning is visible, since much loss occurs before it is noticed.
principles.quote: Start before you can see thinning.

sources.title: How I Reversed My Hair Loss: Bryan Johnson's multi-layer hair regrowth protocol
sources.originalTitle: How I Reversed My Hair Loss

principles.text: Start a hair health protocol early, before loss is visible.
principles.quote: Consider starting a hair health protocol before you can visibly detect loss.

sources.summary: Bryan details how he reversed receding gums, eroding teeth and bruxism over three years on Blueprint. He explains which dental baselines to measure, his nine-step daily oral care routine, and hygiene tips on sugar, acid, hydration and brushing timing.

principles.text: See the dentist at least twice a year to catch problems and remove hardened plaque.

sources.summary: Bryan Johnson and the Blueprint clinical team outline seven free at-home fitness tests (push-ups, sit-rise, waist-to-height, grip strength, sit-and-reach, one-leg stand, reaction time) whose results are entered in the Don't Die app to get a biological age. principles.text: Biological age can be estimated for free at home with seven simple fitness tests, entered into the Don't Die app.

principles.text: Waist-to-height ratio is a measure of body fat distribution and metabolic risk; smaller is better.

principles.text: Grip strength is tracked as a marker correlating with cardiovascular disease risk; higher is better.

principles.text: Test endurance, balance and reaction speed: push-ups, one-leg stand with eyes shut, and best-of-five reaction time.

sources.title: Speed of aging: how Bryan hit 0.48 and why DNA methylation anchors the Rejuvenation Olympics
sources.originalTitle: I Have the World's Slowest Speed of Aging
sources.summary: Bryan reports a 0.48 speed of aging (PACE, DNA methylation), ranking #1 of 5,677 Rejuvenation Olympics competitors. He explains why he built a data-first leaderboard to replace anecdote-driven health advice, argues methodical work can beat genetic gifts, and outlines how to compete with three tests within two years.

principles.text: Health decisions should rest on rigorous science, measurement and data, not storytelling and anecdote.
principles.quote: health influencers and health fads were primarily storytelling-based and anecdotal. What was missing: rigorous science, measurement and data.

principles.text: DNA methylation (PACE) is a comprehensive whole-body aging signal, broader than single markers like glucose or cholesterol.
principles.quote: DNA methylation is a whole-body health marker that integrates thousands of biochemical cues into a measurable signal.

principles.text: Blueprint's core protocol is built on population-level evidence and applies to everyone, with optional individual customization.
principles.quote: We built Blueprint on population level scientific evidence. So it’s not an accurate criticism that Blueprint is based upon my biomarkers.

principles.text: Genetics matter, but methodical hard work can meaningfully slow aging, even beating genetically gifted people.
principles.quote: through methodical hard work, one can meaningfully slow down their speed of aging, even outperforming all the genetically gifted ones.

principles.text: Treat rejuvenation like a sport: understand the science, design evidence-based protocols, execute with precision.
principles.quote: I’ve loved playing this game of trying to understand the science, design evidence based protocols, and then execute with precision.

principles.text: Verified leaderboard rank uses your best three tests within two years, allowing experimentation without punishing the learning process.
principles.quote: Your best 3 test results within 2 years will be displayed, allowing for experimentation with various interventions and protocols while not punishing you for the learning process.

sources.title: Sauna Protocol: Bryan's daily dry sauna routine and how to copy it at home
sources.summary: Bryan ran a 30-day dry sauna experiment and calls sauna one of the most efficacious longevity protocols he has done. He shares his own protocol (200°F, 20 min, daily), a home version (80-100°C, 15-20 min, 3-5x/week), his toxin, microplastic, vascular and fertility results, and safety cautions.

principles.text: Dry sauna is a high-value longevity protocol: 15-20 min, 3-7x a week, at 176-212°F (80-100°C).
principles.quote: dry sauna is great for longevity - do 15-20 min, 3-7x a week, 176-212°F (80-100°C)

principles.text: Bryan saunas daily at 200°F for 20 min in the morning after his workout.
principles.quote: Type: Dry sauna Temperature: 200°F (93°C) Relative air humidity: very low, 5-20% Duration: 20 min Frequency: Daily When: In the morning after my workout

principles.text: Long-term frequent sauna use is linked to markedly lower all-cause mortality.
principles.quote: Using a dry sauna 4+ times per week is linked to about a 40% lower risk of dying from any cause, compared to not using a sauna, based on long-term studies.

principles.text: Men should ice the testicles during sauna; without ice his fertility markers dropped sharply.
principles.quote: Most importantly for men, ice the boys. Icing the testicles prevents heat from damaging fertility markers.

principles.text: Beginners should aim for the lower end of the temperature range; very high heat causes side effects.
principles.quote: Aim for the lower end of this spectrum, especially as a beginner. Higher temperatures closer to the boiling point can cause side effects like headaches and severely dried nose and eyes.

principles.text: Never sauna dehydrated; rehydrate with water plus electrolytes afterward and shower to wash off toxins.
principles.quote: Never use a sauna when dehydrated, and drink plenty of water afterwards to rehydrate. In general, you might need to rehydrate with up to 16-32 oz (0.5-1 L) of fluid after a sauna session.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's simplified 2026 morning routine: 4h46m, 5 am wake, 90 min exercise
sources.summary: Bryan walks through his current morning routine, which his team stripped down after scrutinizing every step. It covers 8:30 pm bedtime, light and breath work, a pre-workout stack, 90 min of exercise, daily sauna, red/NIR light, hair and skin care, and a plant-based breakfast. He stresses starting small rather than copying him.

principles.text: Sleep is the top priority; the day starts the night before with an 8:30 pm bedtime.
principles.quote: Every day starts the night before. Sleep is my #1 life priority because high-quality rest makes hard things easy and impossible things doable.

principles.text: Audit every routine step and cut what doesn't earn its place; simplify over time.
principles.quote: We scrutinized every step to determine whether or not it belonged in the routine.

principles.text: Use bright 10,000 lux light for 6 min when waking before sunrise to support circadian rhythm.
principles.quote: Since I wake up before sunrise, I use a 10,000 lux light for 6 min to simulate natural morning light. This helps to support my circadian rhythm (body clock).

principles.text: Exercise 90 min daily, mixing cardio, strength, balance/stretching and HIIT twice a week.
principles.quote: I exercise for 90 min. My workout is a mixture of:

principles.text: Daily 20 min sauna at 200°F, with protections like cooling the face and neck and a wool hat.
principles.quote: I sauna for 20 min daily.

principles.text: Start small rather than copying his routine; let small improvements compound.
principles.quote: If you're struggling, start small. A short walk. 5 min of meditation. 1 better meal. Then let the improvements compound.

sources.title: Bryan Johnson's evening routine: 9 protocols for 3-minute sleep onset
sources.summary: Bryan explains how he falls asleep within 3 minutes nightly, ranking in the 99.4th sleep percentile. The routine centers on a noon final meal, HRV breathing, dim red/amber light, a 60-minute screen-free wind-down, and a consistent 8:30 pm bedtime, with advice to start small.

principles.text: Finish eating early; it's the single most impactful sleep change. Bryan's last meal is around noon.
principles.quote:
My final meal is around noon. That's ~8.5 hours before I sleep.

This is the single most impactful change I made.

principles.text: Eating near bed raises resting heart rate and cuts sleep quality; digestion conflicts with deep sleep.
principles.quote: When I eat close to bed, my resting heart rate before sleep climbs to 52-56 beats per min (bpm) and I lose roughly 30% of my sleep quality.

principles.text: Build up gradually: finish food 2, then 3, then 4 hours before bed, and check your data each morning.
principles.quote: Start by finishing food 2 hours before bed. Move to 3 hours. Then 4. Each step forward shows up in your data the next morning.

principles.text: Do 10 minutes of 4:6 breathing before bed to raise HRV and calm the nervous system.
principles.quote: I do 10 min of 4:6 breathing before bed. That's breathing in through the nose for 4 seconds and out for 6.

principles.text: Turn screens off 60 minutes before bed and wind down with family, walking, or reading a real book.
principles.quote: I turn off screens 60 min before bed and enable Sleep Bryan.

principles.text: Keep a consistent bedtime within +/- 30 minutes, timed to allow 7-9 hours of sleep.
principles.quote: Choose a time that allows you to get 7-9 hours of sleep. Go to bed within +/- 30 min of this time every night.

sources.originalTitle: Things That Make You Age Faster and Slower
sources.summary: Bryan reacts to a study of 16 epigenetic age clocks across many interventions and maps the results to his own protocol. He explains why he stopped rapamycin, keeps metformin, avoids grains, trusts the DunedinPACE clock, and why single clocks and rodent data are unreliable proxies for human longevity.

principles.text: Continuous measurement of real biomarkers and performance indicators converges on the interventions that best slow epigenetic aging.
principles.quote: continuous measurement and optimization for actual biomarkers and performance indicators automatically consolidates the interventions that best slow down epigenetic biological age.

principles.text: He stopped rapamycin because his own labs showed metabolic side effects, and the clock data did not support it.
principles.quote: In September I stopped Rapamycin, based on concerns around its metabolic side-effects observed in my lab results (including increased cholesterol, blood sugar and RHR)

principles.text: He continues metformin, seeing it as a promising longevity intervention: 5 of 16 clocks improved and none worsened.
principles.quote: 5 out of the 16 clocks indicating significant reduction/deceleration in biological age, with no clock indicating the contrary.

principles.text: A green Mediterranean diet slowed aging on the most clocks and is closest to his Blueprint diet; he stays grain-free.
principles.quote: A green mediterranean diet fared best at reducing/slowing down aging as measured by 10 out of 16 aging clocks, this diet is the closest to my Blueprint diet.

principles.text: He tracks biological age with the DunedinPACE clock, which he considers the most reliable and sensitive, especially in healthy people.
principles.quote: I continuously trace my epigenetic biological age using the PACE (DunedinPACE) clock, as discussed this clock is superior in both reliability and sensitivity

principles.text: Rodent lifespan data is a weak predictor of what works in humans; rapamycin is the example.
principles.quote: This further puts to question the validity of rodent data in predicting longevity interventions in humans.

principles.text: Take your shoes off at the door to keep outdoor contaminants out of your body.
principles.quote: Once these contaminants are inside your house, they're far more likely to get inside your body.

principles.text: Measure indoor air quality and make the HVAC filter your first line of defense, using the highest MERV your system supports.
principles.quote: Your HVAC system should be your first line of defense for air quality. Upgrade your filter and clean it regularly.

principles.text: Clean your water with reverse osmosis that includes a remineralization step.
principles.quote: Make sure your reverse osmosis system includes a remineralization step for electrolyte balance.

principles.text: Swap non-stick pans for stainless steel or cast iron to avoid PFAS.
principles.quote: Use stainless steel or cast iron pans instead.

principles.text: Use dim red light in the evening and block light and noise in the bedroom to protect sleep.
principles.quote: Use a dim red light ~2 hours before bed to help your body wind down and prepare for sleep.

principles.text: Don't be anxious about toxins; remove the big ones gradually.
principles.quote: Be patient with yourself. It took me 5 years to improve my home environment.

sources.title: Why Bryan Johnson stopped taking rapamycin after almost 5 years
sources.summary: Bryan explains his decision to end almost five years of rapamycin experimentation. Across weekly, biweekly and alternating protocols, the side effects (infections, lipid and glucose changes, higher resting heart rate) outweighed the longevity benefits, and new epigenetic clock data added to the concern.

principles.text: Stop a longevity compound when the side effects outweigh the benefits, even after years of use.
principles.quote: the benefits of lifelong dosing of Rapamycin do not justify the hefty side-effects (intermittent skin/soft tissue infections, lipid abnormalities, glucose elevations, and increased resting heart rate).

principles.text: Test multiple dosing protocols before judging a molecule, and adjust dose before quitting.
principles.quote: I have tested various rapamycin protocols including weekly (5, 6, and 10 mg dose schedules), biweekly (13 mg), and alternating weekly (6/13 mg) to optimize rejuvenation and limit side effects.

principles.text: If a suspected cause persists after dose adjustments, discontinue it entirely.
principles.quote: With no other underlying causes identified, we suspected Rapamycin, and since dosage adjustments had no effect, we decided to discontinue it entirely.

principles.text: Prolonged rapamycin use raises concerns about metabolism and long-run cancer immune surveillance.
principles.quote: Despite anecdotal evidence of rapamycin slowing down tumor growth, its effect in inhibiting natural killer cells [4] raises concerns for anti-cancer immune surveillance and cancer risk in the longer run.

principles.text: Judge interventions across many aging clocks, not one or two, to avoid cherry-picked results.
principles.quote: most longevity interventions up to date have been tested against one or two aging clocks, leading to invisible biases and potential intended “cherry picking” of favorable clocks for the tested interventions.

principles.text: Keep watching the research and your own biomarkers constantly, since longevity science keeps evolving.
principles.quote: Longevity research around these experimental compounds is constantly evolving, necessitating ongoing, close observation of the research and my biomarkers, which my team and I do constantly.

principles.text: Measure every organ, then maximally reverse each one's quantified biological age.

principles.text: Let biomarker data, not the conscious mind, decide what to eat; remove willpower from the loop.
