chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan lays out ten habits behind eight months of 100% perfect sleep: treat sleep as priority one, wind down, manage light and temperature, keep a fixed bedtime, eat early, skip stimulants, and track data. He backs it with sleep-deprivation research and his own data on meal timing and resting heart rate.

chunks.heading: Sleep as the top priority
chunks.text:
- Bryan says high-quality sleep changed his life. It took years to build the habits behind eight months of 100% perfect sleep, which he believes is the best in the world.
- His advice: "If you only do one thing for your health: sleep."
- He tells people to see themselves as "a professional sleeper": make sleep the #1 priority, plan the day around it, treat it as the most important calendar appointment, and get buy-in from others by explaining the priority.
- He dismisses the idea that sleep is for the weak; those people are "drunk from sleep deprivation."

chunks.heading: Why sleep deprivation matters
chunks.text:
- Being awake for 18 or 24 hours is equivalent to a blood alcohol content of 0.05% or 0.1%. In the U.S., 0.08% is legally intoxicated.
- Averaging six hours of sleep or less makes you 4.2x more likely to develop the common cold.
- After one night with 4 hours of sleep, natural killer cell activity fell 70% in 18 of 23 participants. One night of normal sleep restored it to baseline. NK cells kill cancer cells, among other functions.
- Preclinical studies link lack of sleep to inhibited immune surveillance and increased tumor growth in animal models.
- Sleep deprivation also reduces cognition, slows reflexes and worsens decision-making. It is linked to heart disease, diabetes, obesity, anxiety, depression and weakened immunity.

chunks.heading: Wind-down routine (30-60 minutes)
chunks.text:
Set a specific time each evening to start winding down. Options he lists, with the evidence he cites:

- Relaxing activities such as reading or a warm bath. An online randomized trial of 991 subjects found reading a book in bed improved self-reported sleep quality in a majority of participants.
- Mindfulness or deep breathing. A wide meta-analysis found mindfulness meditation outperformed controls and was equivalent to medications for sleep disturbances.
- Soothing music. In a study of 94 students, calming classical music beat a negative control and an audiobook for sleep quality and depression. A meta-analysis of 9 studies with 489 older adults showed improvements in sleep latency, duration and efficiency.

chunks.heading: Light management
chunks.text:
**Morning**
- Get outside within 15-30 minutes of waking to set the circadian rhythm and boost mood.
- Use a light therapy device if natural sunlight isn't available.

**Evening**
- Dim lights one to two hours before bed and use warm lighting; red light is even better.
- Install blue light filters on devices (e.g. f.lux) and consider blue light-blocking glasses.
- Limit screens for at least an hour before bed and black out the bedroom.

chunks.heading: Bedtime consistency and sleep environment
chunks.text:
- Pick a bedtime that allows 7-9 hours in bed, and keep it consistent, including weekends. Avoid scheduling late nights.
- Set an alarm for winding down.
- Keep the bedroom between 60-67°F (15-19°C). Use breathable bedding and light sleepwear, fans or cooling devices, ventilation, and a temperature-controlled mattress if possible. A warm bath before bed can help.
- Keep the room quiet, dark, cool, clean and clutter-free, with a comfortable mattress and pillows. Use a noise machine or earplugs if needed.

chunks.heading: Meal timing
chunks.text:
- After years of testing, Bryan landed on an 11 am final meal as best for sleep. He goes to bed at 8:30 pm, by which time primary digestion is done and his resting heart rate is about 47-49 bpm.
- If he eats later, his resting heart rate is 55-58 bpm because he is still digesting, and sleep quality drops by about 30%.
- For others: eat the last meal at least two hours before bed and avoid large meals near bedtime. Experiment with 4 and 6 hours and see whether sleep improves.
- Late eating creates large metabolic demands, causes blood glucose fluctuations, reduces melatonin production, and disrupts the natural drop in core body temperature.
- He found foods like pasta and bread reduced his sleep quality, and was surprised how much food affected sleep both positively and negatively.

chunks.heading: Stimulants
chunks.text:
- He suggests avoiding caffeine, alcohol and other stimulants at least 10 hours before sleep. He consumes neither, because each disrupts his mood and sleep.
- Caffeine has a 6-hour half-life, so coffee 6 hours before bed is like half a cup right before bed.
- Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, which stops the brain sensing declining energy that it needs to switch to sleep mode. It can also interfere with sleep phases later in the night.
- Alcohol may speed falling asleep, but it reduces REM sleep, increases fragmentation (frequent awakenings) and can worsen existing medical conditions.
- Evening alternative: herbal teas or other relaxing drinks.

chunks.heading: Track and iterate
chunks.text:
- Track sleep with a journal or sleep tracker, use the data to adjust the routine, and keep monitoring and tweaking.
- He frames it as a journey: take it one step at a time, starting with reshaping your relationship with sleep.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan argues heart rate before sleep (HRBS) is the single most important health metric and a longevity lever, because it predicts sleep quality. He explains how to measure it, what a good score is, and gives a protocol of food, caffeine, exercise, stress and light habits that lowers it.

chunks.heading: Heart rate before sleep (HRBS) as Bryan's top health metric
chunks.text:
Bryan's #1 health tip is to lower heart rate before sleep (HRBS): "I've spent millions of dollars developing health protocols backed by science. I do dozens of things a day for my health. But if you're going to focus on one thing, it would be this." He calls it "the most consequential health lesson to learn," and says it can be improved immediately and for free.

- HRBS is the number of heartbeats per minute while lying quietly right before sleep.
- He treats it as a single-number biomarker of overall health. It reveals fitness, metabolic health, food habits and stress management.
- After five years of health experimentation, it is the marker he focuses on most, because it "mirrors how I'm doing in life generally."
- He also treats it as a longevity therapy in its own right, not just a measurement.

chunks.heading: Why a low HRBS matters
chunks.text:
- A lower heart rate reflects activation of the parasympathetic ("rest and digest") system, which promotes relaxation and sleep onset.
- Lower HRBS makes it more likely to fall asleep faster and get deeper, higher-quality sleep.
- Example he gives: after a large meal before bed, heart rate stays elevated as the body diverts energy to digestion, making it harder to fall and stay asleep.
- He calls sleep "the #1 longevity therapy." Poor sleep is linked to:
  - higher risk of death
  - increased hunger and weight gain
  - increased risk of hypertension
  - irritability and impaired judgement
  - lower functional IQ by 12-15 points
- His personal data point: resting heart rate before bed is the strongest predictor of his sleep quality. At 40 bpm he is "guaranteed a perfect night's sleep." At 57 bpm he loses about 30% of sleep quality, "every time."

chunks.heading: How to measure HRBS
chunks.text:
- Lie flat on your back and relax for sixty seconds. He finds a few deep breaths helpful to calm the body.
- With a wearable, check the app.
- Without one, count your pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 (e.g. 70 bpm).

chunks.heading: What counts as a good score
chunks.text:
- Around 50 bpm is a "fantastic" HRBS. It reflects an efficient heart and a nervous system in "rest" mode, common in aerobically fit people and athletes.
- It can signal good stroke volume, higher vagal tone and better cardiorespiratory fitness.
- His own HRBS usually hovers between 39-44 bpm.
- If yours is in the 60s, 70s, 80s or 90s, he says meaningful progress can come very quickly. Measure baseline tonight, then lower it gradually.
- Safety notes he gives: if the score is consistently below 40 or above 80, especially with symptoms, check with a physician. Seek care for dizziness or fainting. Women typically run about 3 bpm higher.

chunks.heading: The general HRBS protocol
chunks.text:
Bryan notes his own protocol is "over-the-top for most people" because he is intensely focused on longevity, so he recommends this baseline for others:

- Finish all food about 4 hours before bed (earlier is better).
- Avoid heavy or large foods at the last meals (e.g. pasta).
- Avoid alcohol entirely.
- Avoid blue light, including screens, at least 1 hour before bed (screens off 60 minutes before).
- Avoid stress close to bed (fights, working late).
- Finish all caffeine or stimulants by 12pm.
- Finish high-intensity exercise 4 hours before bed.
- Have a calming routine 1 hour before bed (read, walk, journal).
- Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
- Keep the same bedtime every night.

chunks.heading: What raises resting heart rate before bed
chunks.text:
Bryan lists approximate increases in bpm:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Alcohol before bedtime | +5-10 bpm |
| Anxiety, stress, rumination | +5-25 bpm |
| Late-day caffeine | +2-5 bpm |
| Intense evening exercise | +4-10 bpm |
| Large evening meals | +10 bpm |
| Nicotine | +10 bpm |
| Dehydration | +5 bpm |
| High room or body temperature | +5 bpm |
| Certain medications | +7 bpm |

chunks.heading: Bryan's extra personal tactics
chunks.text:
- Slight caloric restriction at 2,250 calories daily.
- Finishes all food by 12pm.
- Uses only red light in the house at night.

chunks.heading: Results, compounding and adoption
chunks.text:
- Results come quickly because the body responds almost immediately, and the benefits scaffold: a lower HRBS tonight means better sleep tomorrow, which means a lower heart rate tomorrow night.
- He describes it as "simple, measurable, and entirely within your control." Friends tell him it has changed their life.
- He admits he is asking a lot, such as turning off screens and eating earlier in a culture that eats late. His promise: "You will feel more vibrant and energetic."
- Social tactic: at events where you need to fit in, eat lightly. He advises small daily steps, and argues individual behavior can shift culture toward a new norm.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan explains how he reached eight months of perfect sleep scores by treating sleep as a top priority. He covers meal timing, light exposure, wind-down routines, consistent bedtimes and managing caffeine.

chunks.heading: Core principle: build life around sleep
chunks.text:
Bryan calls sleep "the most powerful drug available – for performance, mental health, and well-being." He says it is the topic he gets asked about most. After years of struggling, he reports achieving the best sleep score in the world: "Eight months of perfect sleep."

- Sleep is treated as an afterthought in culture (after the movie, after work, "when you feel like it").
- He argues it deserves the same seriousness and devotion as work, because it "demands your best performance."
- His framing: build your life around sleep, not sleep around your life.

chunks.heading: Final meal timing and resting heart rate
chunks.text:
Bryan's rule is to finish the last meal at least two hours before bed.

- Example: with a 10 PM bedtime, finish eating by 8 PM.
- To adapt, move the final meal back 30 minutes each day. By the end of the first week, the last meal lands around 5 PM.
- The purpose is to lower resting heart rate by giving the body time to digest and prepare for sleep.
- His claim: "The lower your resting heart rate, the better your sleep."

chunks.heading: Light: avoid blue light before bed
chunks.text:
- An hour or two before bed, avoid blue light.
- Options: turn off screens, or remove blue light from them using apps and settings on computers and mobile devices.
- Replace it with red and amber lighting.
- He says light significantly affects readiness to fall asleep.

chunks.heading: Wind-down routine and separation from work
chunks.text:
Bryan argues you can't finish work and put your head on the pillow and expect great sleep. You must calm body and mind, and create "separation from work."

- Options he lists: read a book, go for a walk, do a breathing exercise, take a bath, meditate, or journal.
- His own method is an internal dialogue where he splits himself into characters such as "Ambitious Bryan" and "Anxious Bryan."
  - Each part is allowed to voice the pressing things on its mind.
  - He writes them down and tells each part he hears it and will address it tomorrow, after a great night's sleep.
  - He finds it helpful to separate into parts and empathize with each one's concerns and objectives.

chunks.heading: Consistency of bedtime
chunks.text:
- The body loves routine and rewards it with strong sleep performance.
- Go to bed within +/- 30 minutes of your chosen bedtime every single day.
- Build the habit and stay with it.

chunks.heading: Stimulants and caffeine timing
chunks.text:
- Caffeine has a six-hour half-life. Example: coffee at 4 PM leaves about half a coffee in your system at a 10 PM bedtime.
- People metabolize caffeine differently, so the right cutoff is individual.
- His guidance: err on the side of caution and take stimulants earlier in the day.

chunks.heading: Mindset on sleep difficulty
chunks.text:
- Bryan says "Sleep is hard work" and success takes time, like all things.
- His closing advice: invest in the habits and the body will perform.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan lays out his weekly exercise framework: consistency over intensity, four categories (strength, zone 2, HIIT, mobility), his weekly targets, a sample 7-day routine, and pre/post-workout nutrition with Blueprint products. He stresses that even 11 minutes a day matters.

chunks.heading: Exercise priorities and weekly structure
chunks.text:
Bryan says no single exercise is best; a mix is. Each week he focuses on four categories:
- strength training
- low-intensity cardio (zone 2 heart rate)
- high-intensity cardio (zone 4 or 5)
- mobility, flexibility, and balance

He cites a study linking 11 minutes of daily exercise to a 23% lower risk of early death. His message: a small daily habit produces meaningful benefits, and consistency matters more than going all out once a month. "Even 10 minutes a day is a big win." He also says: "Don't get caught up in all the nuances and rabbit holes of exercise."

chunks.heading: Ground rules for training
chunks.text:
- **Strength:** aim for 2-3 sessions a week using compound movements (squats, deadlifts, lunges). If three is too much, even one session is a win.
- **Progressive overload:** gradually raise the weight or reps over time. Consistency takes you a long way.
- **HIIT as best return on time:** 4-6 reps of 30-second all-out efforts with rest between, 3 times a week, can match the cardiovascular gains of 5 weekly sessions of 40-60 minutes of steady cardio. He notes cardiorespiratory fitness is one of the strongest predictors of lifespan, and that intervals are the best trade when time is tight.
- **Timing:** avoid high-intensity exercise within 4 hours of bed, since research suggests it reduces sleep quality and recovery.

chunks.heading: Bryan's own weekly targets
chunks.text:
He does a mix of strength, cardio, balance, and flexibility every day, aiming for:
- at least 150 minutes of zone 2 cardio per week
- at least 75 minutes of high-intensity cardio per week (about 10 minutes of that at near-max effort)
- mobility, flexibility, and balance training every day

chunks.heading: Sample week: strength days (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)
chunks.text:
**Monday (~60 min, strength plus moderate cardio):**
- 5 min general warm-up, 5 min dynamic warm-up
- 20 min strength: squats 3x10-15, push-ups 3x8-12, single-arm dumbbell rows 3x10-12, kettlebell swings and/or farmer's walks 3x30 seconds, planks 3x20-30 seconds
- 5-10 min stability work (single-leg balance, bird dog, single-leg RDL, dead bugs, plank with shoulder taps)
- 25 min moderate cardio (brisk walking, jogging, cycling, swimming, elliptical)

**Wednesday (60 min, strength, flexibility, balance, mobility):**
- 10 min dynamic stretching
- 30 min compound strength targeting areas not sore from Monday
- 15 min yoga (cat-cow, cobbler's pose, tree pose, cobra pose)
- 5 min static stretching cooldown

**Friday (45-60 min, strength):**
- 5 min general plus 5 min dynamic warm-up
- lunges 3x10, overhead press 3x10, dumbbell chest press 3x10, side plank 20-30 seconds each side, step-ups 3x10 each leg
- 5-10 min stability work

chunks.heading: Sample week: HIIT days (Tuesday, Thursday)
chunks.text:
**Tuesday (~10 min HIIT plus moderate cardio):**
- 8 rounds of 20 seconds all-out, 20 seconds rest or very low intensity (40 seconds rest for beginners), about 5 minutes total
- run, cycle, or use bodyweight exercises
- fill remaining time with moderate cardio at 60-70% of max heart rate, a pace where you can hold a conversation but still feel the effort

**Thursday (~40 min, Norwegian 4x4):**
- 10 min warm-up building to a light sweat
- 4 rounds of 4 min hard at about 85-95% of max heart rate (zone 4-5, unable to hold a conversation by the last minute), then 3 min easy at zone 2
- 5 min cooldown with a few static stretches
- use joint-friendly modes: cycling, rowing, incline treadmill walking, stair climber

Pointers: the hard 4 minutes should feel "uncomfortable but controlled, not an all-out sprint," paced so the fourth interval matches the first. If four rounds is too much, start with two or three. Finish at least 4 hours before bed.

chunks.heading: Sample week: weekend
chunks.text:
- **Saturday:** play with friends (hiking, biking, swimming, pickleball with caution, basketball).
- **Sunday (35-50 min active recovery):** 20-30 min gentle yoga or stretching with extra mobility work, plus 15-20 min mindfulness meditation.

He says you could instead do some strength and cardio every day, or spread it out: "Do what works for you."

chunks.heading: Pre- and post-workout nutrition
chunks.text:
General guidance: eat 1-2 hours before exercise (complex carbs plus some protein), and eat complex carbs plus protein ideally within 1 hour after.

**Bryan's pre-workout:**
- an 8-oz drink with Longevity Mix and Creatine
- Longevity Protein eaten with Blueberry Nut Mix, Collagen Peptides, extra virgin olive oil, and berries
- then he exercises

**Bryan's post-workout:** a meal with veggies, legumes, extra virgin olive oil, berries, nuts, and seeds.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan Johnson lists 14 recipes he's been eating lately, calling food one of life's greatest joys. They are plant-based dishes built around vegetables, lentils, chickpeas, mushrooms, cauliflower and squash, with weighed gram quantities, olive oil, nuts and seeds, plus a porridge and a berry smoothie. The essay gives ingredients only and no stated principles.

chunks.heading: Vegetable stir fry with cauliflower rice
chunks.text:
Bryan lists this as one of the recipes he eats regularly, calling eating "one of life's greatest joys." Quantities are by weight:

- Vegetables: 1/2 medium onion (about 75 g), 1/4 red cabbage and 1/4 white cabbage (about 150 g each), 200 g mung bean sprouts, 200 g broccoli, 225 g shiitake mushrooms, 150 g sugar snap peas.
- Seasoning: 15 g ginger powder, 15 g garlic powder, 30 ml gluten-free low-sodium tamari.
- Base: 600 g cauliflower rice, cooked in 15 ml olive oil.
- Optional garnish: 7 g hemp seeds.

chunks.heading: Soups: lemon red lentil and butternut squash
chunks.text:
**Lemon red lentil soup**
- 15-30 ml olive oil, 3 large carrots (about 360 g), 2 celery stalks (about 180 g), 1 yellow onion (about 150 g), 4 cloves garlic.
- 1.5 liters vegetable stock, 225 g red lentils, 2 bay leaves.
- 2.5 g turmeric, 5 g cumin, juice of 1 lemon, optional lemon zest.

**Butternut squash soup with roasted apples and carrots (serves 4-6)**
- 1 onion, 3 garlic cloves, 1 butternut squash (about 4 cups cubed), 2 Honeycrisp apples, 2 large carrots.
- 1 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp ginger powder.
- 4 cups vegetable broth, 1 cup coconut milk, 2 tbsp olive oil.

chunks.heading: Chickpea-based dishes: frittata, stew and chickpea rice bowl
chunks.text:
**Chickpea vegetable frittata**
- 240 g chickpea flour and 360 ml water form the egg-free base.
- 1/2 onion, 2 red peppers, 1 zucchini, 1 bunch each of parsley and chives, 2 garlic cloves, 1 Roma tomato, 225 g mushrooms.
- 15 g garlic powder, 15 g ground cumin, 15 ml olive oil.

**Chickpea stew**
- 5 garlic cloves, 2 tbsp (30 mL) extra virgin olive oil, 2 tbsp (30 g) tomato paste.
- Spices: 1 tbsp (6-8 g) cumin, 1 tbsp (6-8 g) paprika, 1 tsp (3 g) red pepper flakes, 2-3 tsp (5-7 g) za'atar, 2-3 bay leaves.
- 3 cups (500 g) cooked chickpeas, 1 roasted bell pepper.

**Black bean and mushroom bowl with chickpea rice (serves 2-3)**
- 1 can (15 oz) black beans, 1 cup cherry tomatoes, 1/2 onion, 1 cup oyster mushrooms.
- Seasoning: 1 tsp umami seasoning, 1/2 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp olive oil.
- Toppings: 1/4 cup pickled red onions, 1 cup spinach, 1/2 cup shredded carrots, 1/2 cup sliced radish, 1/4 cup cilantro.
- Served over 1 1/2 cups cooked chickpea rice.

chunks.heading: Plant-based "meat" dishes: lentil loaf, walnut bolognese and cauliflower "turkey"
chunks.text:
**Cauliflower lentil loaf**
- Loaf: 200 g cooked lentils, 300 g riced cauliflower, 150 g onion, 8 oz mushrooms, 30 g nutritional yeast.
- Seasoning: 5 g minced garlic, 5 g Dijon mustard, 2.5 g smoked paprika, 2.5 g cumin, 1.5 g black pepper, 1.5 g chipotle powder.
- Glaze: 80 ml unsweetened ketchup and 5 ml liquid smoke.

**Mushroom and walnut bolognese with spaghetti squash**
- 225 g cremini mushrooms, 40 g each of onion, carrot and celery, 2 garlic cloves, 60 g walnuts.
- 15 g garlic powder, 15 g Italian seasoning, 15 g tomato paste, 340 g tomato sauce.
- 30 ml gluten-free tamari, 30 ml balsamic vinegar.
- Served on a roasted medium spaghetti squash (about 1/2 squash), with 5 ml olive oil for greasing.

**Herb-seasoned cauliflower "turkey" with sweet potato mash and green beans**
- "Turkey": 1 large cauliflower head, 30 ml olive oil, 10 g each of garlic powder, onion powder and smoked paprika, 5 g each of dried thyme and rosemary, 15 g nutritional yeast, 100 ml vegetable broth for basting.
- Sweet potato mash: 800 g sweet potatoes, 30-60 ml plant milk, 5 g garlic powder, 5 g cinnamon.
- Green beans: 400 g, blanched in ice water.

chunks.heading: Squash, lentil and curry dishes
chunks.text:
**Mushroom walnut stuffed acorn squash**
- 2 medium acorn squash, halved, with 1 tbsp olive oil.
- Filling: 1 tbsp olive oil, 16 oz crimini mushrooms, 4 tbsp walnuts, 4 tbsp unsweetened dried cranberries, 1 tbsp honey, 1/2 tbsp cinnamon.

**Black lentil and olive salad with spiced roasted carrots and sun-dried tomato hummus**
- Carrots: 3 large carrots, 1 shallot, 2 tbsp olive oil, 1 tbsp maple syrup, 1 tsp each of smoked paprika and cumin, 1/2 tsp salt.
- Salad: 1 cup black lentils cooked in 2 cups water or broth, 1 tbsp red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon, 1/4 cup black currants, 1/2 cup Castelvetrano olives, 1/3 cup roasted almonds, 1/4 cup parsley, 2 tbsp mint.
- Served with 1/2 cup sun-dried tomato hummus.

**Sweet potato and cabbage curry with cauliflower rice**
- 2 cups shredded cabbage, 1 small/medium sweet potato (1-inch pieces), 1 onion, 2 tbsp olive oil.
- Spices: 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 dry red chili, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander, 1/2 tsp red chili powder, 1/2 tsp salt.
- Finish with 1/4 cup cilantro and 1 tbsp lime juice, served over 2 cups cauliflower rice.

chunks.heading: Breakfast and snack: grain-free porridge and superfood smoothie
chunks.text:
**Grain-free porridge with butterfly pea flower**
- 250 ml macadamia nut milk, 30 g almond flour, 15 g hemp seeds, 10 g chia seeds, 10 g ground flax.
- 1/2 tsp vanilla, 1 tsp butterfly pea flower powder, 1/4 tsp cardamom.
- Blend until smooth and top with a handful of fresh berries.

**Superfood smoothie (serves 1-2)**
- 1/2 cup each of strawberries, blueberries and pitted dark cherries, 1/4 cup pomegranate arils.
- 1 cup almond milk, 1 tbsp flax seeds, 5-6 macadamia nuts, 1 tsp chia seeds, 1 tsp Blueprint cacao.
- Blend until smooth.

chunks.heading: Patterns across Bryan's recipes
chunks.text:
- Every recipe is plant-based and built on vegetables, legumes, mushrooms, nuts and seeds.
- Cauliflower rice, spaghetti squash and chickpea rice stand in for grains and pasta.
- Olive oil is the main fat, with garlic, cumin, smoked paprika and turmeric as staple seasonings.
- Sugar is minimal. Ketchup is unsweetened, cranberries are unsweetened, and sweeteners appear only in small amounts (1 tbsp honey, 1 tbsp maple syrup).
- Ingredients are weighed in grams, in line with his measured, protocol-driven approach.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan shares the exact recipe and cooking method for Super Veggie, the meal he eats every day. It combines black lentils, cruciferous vegetables, mushrooms and spices, cooked at low temperature with high humidity and acidity to limit AGEs and ALEs.

chunks.heading: Super Veggie: what it is and why Bryan eats it
chunks.text:
- Bryan eats "Super Veggie" every day as his lunch and says "I love it."
- He frames the food as delicious to him and "one of the most exciting moments of my day."
- He notes that newcomers may need a period of adaptation, and some will want to tweak the recipe or texture.
- He adds that Blueprint "breaks all kinds of social norms," which predictably triggers human reactions.

chunks.heading: Super Veggie ingredients and quantities
chunks.text:
- Black lentils: 45 g dry, about 150 g cooked
- Broccoli (head and stalk): 250 g (broccoli sprouts can substitute)
- Cauliflower: 150 g
- Shiitake or maitake mushrooms: 50 g
- Garlic: 1 clove
- Ginger root: 3 g
- Lime: 1
- Cumin: 1 Tbsp
- Apple cider vinegar: 1 Tbsp
- Hemp seeds: 1 Tbsp
- Extra virgin olive oil: 1 Tbsp, drizzled after prep
- Seasoning: NuSalt (potassium chloride)

chunks.heading: Cooking the vegetables
chunks.text:
- Weigh the vegetables first.
- Place broccoli, cauliflower, mushrooms, ginger and garlic in boiling water.
- Boil until tender, 7-9 minutes. Steaming is also acceptable.
- Keep the cooking or steaming water, since it can thin the final texture.

chunks.heading: Cooking the lentils
chunks.text:
- Bring water to a boil in a medium saucepan and add the lentils.
- Reduce heat to low and cook uncovered for 18-20 minutes, until "al dente."
- Drain in a colander and rinse under cold water.

chunks.heading: Blending, serving and finishing
chunks.text:
- Bryan allows either blending or keeping the dish whole.
- To blend: put 1 Tbsp dried cumin, 1 Tbsp apple cider vinegar, 1 fresh lime, the cooked black lentils and the strained cooked vegetables into a high-speed blender until it becomes a thick soup.
- If needed, add some of the vegetable (or steaming) water to thin the texture.
- Top with 1 Tbsp hemp seeds, then drizzle 1 Tbsp of extra virgin olive oil.
- Season with NuSalt (potassium chloride).

chunks.heading: Cooking method rationale: minimizing AGEs and ALEs
chunks.text:
- Bryan cooks by "low temperature, high humidity, high acidity, high antioxidant" methods.
- The stated goal is to minimize formation of Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) and Advanced Lipid Peroxidation End-products (ALEs).
- This is why he boils or steams the vegetables and lentils rather than using dry, high-heat methods, and why acid (apple cider vinegar, lime) and antioxidant-rich ingredients are part of the dish.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan Johnson explains how he rebuilt skin he damaged before 40, improving skin age from an average of 64 to between 37 and 42. He lays out lifestyle basics, a daily topical routine with active ingredients, supportive supplements, pro tips and how he measures skin age with multispectral imaging.

chunks.heading: Skin age results and the baseline damage Bryan started from
chunks.text:
- Until age 40, Bryan says he "kind of destroyed" his skin: sunburns, poor diet, no skincare routine.
- When he started Blueprint, his skin was in the 98th percentile for damage on some markers, with an average skin age of 64.
- His skin age has since improved to between 37 and 42.
- He tracks progress by routinely measuring skin biological age with multispectral imaging (Visia is a popular US choice). It reports UV damage, pore size, dark spots and other indicators. Some wellness clinics offer it.

chunks.heading: Skin basics: lifestyle foundations
chunks.text:
- Exercise.
- Prioritize sleep.
- Eat a healthy, Blueprint-like diet.
- Avoid junk, fried or highly processed foods, cigarettes and vaping.
- He says to get sun earlier in the day and later in the evening, when the UV index is lower.
- Position on sun: "The sun is good for you but not too much and not too little. Just the right amount will do."
- If in direct sun when the UV index is high (10 am to 4 pm), protect with clothing, a UV umbrella, a hat and mineral sunscreen.
- He says that if you lack access to extras like red light therapy, don't worry; the basics are a great place to start.

chunks.heading: Daily skincare routine
chunks.text:
- Face wash morning and night.
- Mineral sunscreen.
- Moisturize body and face.
- Targeted active ingredients:
  - Niacinamide, morning and night, in serums or moisturizers.
  - Vitamin C, morning, typically in a serum.
  - Hyaluronic acid, as desired, usually in a serum or moisturizer.
  - Tretinoin (prescription), at night.
- He advises spotting endocrine disruptors in skincare products: chemicals that may mimic or interfere with the body's hormones, linked with health problems in wildlife and humans.

chunks.heading: Supplements for skin
chunks.text:
- Collagen: 20-30 g daily, paired with vitamin C to boost collagen synthesis.
- Niacinamide: 15 mg, in Blueprint Essential Capsules.
- Hyaluronic acid: 120 mg, in Blueprint Longevity Mix.

chunks.heading: Pro tips for UV and blemish control
chunks.text:
- UV-tinted windows to block 99% of damaging UV rays.
- A UV umbrella during high UV index hours.
- Microdosing Accutane at 40 mg weekly for blemish-free skin. Over-the-counter retinols are an alternative.
- Red light therapy 3x per week.

chunks.heading: Advanced collagen and firmness therapies
chunks.text:
Bryan has been experimenting with these to target collagen production, skin firmness and overall skin health:

- Tixel, for collagen and elastin.
- Sofwave, for collagen and elastin.
- Sculptra, injected in the face, to boost natural collagen production.

chunks.heading: Blueprint skincare product plans

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan lays out the five-part routine he credits for having better hair at 49 than 29, with about 70% of his gray gone. It covers nutrition, Blueprint peptide shampoo and serum, a daily laser cap, oral minoxidil and topical minoxidil, plus advice to start before thinning is visible.

chunks.heading: Bryan's haircare outcome and starting early
chunks.text:
- Bryan says his hair is better at 49 than at 29. He started losing hair and going gray in his late 20s. In his late 40s he reports a full head of hair and about 70% of his gray gone.
- He frames this as personal experience ("Results vary"), not a guarantee.
- He advises starting a hair protocol before thinning is visible.
  - By age 20, about 20% of men already have some visible hair loss.
  - Many people lose up to 50% of their hair before they notice it.
  - By age 50, up to 40% of women have noticeable hair loss.
- His basics: good nutrition, science-backed haircare protocols, and starting treatments early.

chunks.heading: Nutrition for hair
chunks.text:
- Bryan holds that the body needs good food to make good hair. He eats whole foods and avoids processed junk and added sugar.
- Nutrients he prioritizes for hair:
  - protein
  - omega-3
  - iron, selenium, biotin, zinc, and vitamins C, D, and E
- His sources: fruits, vegetables, lentils, nuts, seeds, Longevity Mix, and Essential Capsules.
- He also supplements with high-potency omega-3 and broad-spectrum collagen peptides.
- For people who eat meat, he recommends chicken, turkey, and fatty fish such as salmon or mackerel.

chunks.heading: Peptide shampoo and serum routine (daily)
chunks.text:
He uses the Blueprint haircare stack every day:

1. After regular shampoo, apply 1-2 pumps of Blueprint Peptide Shampoo directly to the scalp. Leave on for 2 minutes, then rinse.
2. Apply Blueprint Peptide Hair Serum and massage it into the scalp with a silicone scrubber for 1-2 minutes to stimulate blood flow.

chunks.heading: 302 Laser Cap (low-level laser therapy)
chunks.text:
- Bryan wears the Blueprint 302 Laser Cap for 6 minutes a day.
- It has a wireless battery pack, so he can go through his morning routine while wearing it.
- Rationale he gives: LLLT (low-level laser therapy) may help support regrowth for pattern hair loss in as little as 16 weeks. The technology can deliver around 2.5x more on-target intensity than LEDs to stimulate follicles.

chunks.heading: Minoxidil: oral and topical
chunks.text:
- **Oral minoxidil:** He started at 2.5 mg and evaluated for side effects. He now takes 3.75 mg a day. He notes it is commonly used to support hair regrowth.
- **Topical minoxidil:** He applies 1 mL of 5% minoxidil to the scalp each night.
- He notes oral minoxidil is a prescription medication. It should be used only under the supervision of a qualified healthcare provider, may cause side effects, and is not appropriate for everyone.
- He points to Immortals Medicine as a way to access oral minoxidil.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan Johnson describes how he regrew a full head of hair and cut gray by about half by age 46. His stack combines nutrition, a custom topical Rx, a red light cap and oral minoxidil, with blood monitoring of DHT. He reports PRP/PRF failed for him and stresses monitoring side effects.

chunks.heading: Why Bryan started his hair protocol early and what he credits
chunks.text:
- Bryan says that genetically he "should be bald." He began losing hair and going gray in his late 20s. At 46 he reports a full head of hair and about 50% of his gray gone.
- His main lesson: start early and be proactive. He made the mistake of acting only after he noticed the loss.
- Context he cites: by age 20 about 20% of men have visible hair loss; many people lose up to 50% of their hair before noticing thinning; by age 50 up to 40% of women have noticeable loss.
- His advice is to consider starting a hair health protocol before loss is visible.
- He frames his protocol as open experimentation. He is doing several things at once, but says others need not. Topical minoxidil 5% alone may be all that is needed for good results.
- He stresses humility: "We're still in the early days of anti-aging and likely know far less than we think we know."

chunks.heading: Nutrition for hair health
chunks.text:
- Bryan says proper nutrition matters for hair.
- Nutrients he lists: adequate protein, omega-3 fatty acids, biotin (vitamin B7), vitamin C, vitamin D, vitamin E, iron and zinc.
- He states the Blueprint supplement stack contains all of these.

chunks.heading: Bryan's custom topical formulation and how he applies it
chunks.text:
- **Dose and routine:** 1 mL applied to the scalp each morning (before bed is also fine). He then massages the scalp for 1-2 minutes with a silicone scrubber to stimulate blood flow.
- **Personalization:** the formulation is based on a genetic test that predicts his response to various ingredients. The company then supplies a custom Rx formulation.
- **His ingredients and strengths:**
  - Minoxidil 7%
  - Cetirizine HCl 1%
  - Latanoprost 0.004%
  - Dutasteride 0.25%
  - Melatonin 0.1%
  - Caffeine 0.2%
  - Tretinoin 0.0125%
  - Vitamin D3 1,000 IU/mL
  - Vitamin E 10 IU/mL
- **Budget option:** topical minoxidil 5%. He notes some people get side effects such as itchy skin or headaches, so monitor for them.

chunks.heading: Why he went back to once-daily topical application
chunks.text:
- Bryan tried applying the topical twice a day (morning and night).
- His recent blood results then showed DHT too low at 5.8 ng/dL, which he says can create side effects.
- He returned to once daily and plans to retest his blood in 90 days.
- The takeaway: track blood markers when using DHT-lowering ingredients such as dutasteride, rather than assuming more application is better.

chunks.heading: Red light cap and oral minoxidil
chunks.text:
- **Red light cap:** six minutes a day. He says you can wear it during your morning routine.
- **Oral minoxidil:** he takes 3.75 mg a day. He started at 2.5 mg and evaluated for side effects before moving up.
- **Evidence he cites:** a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in 90 men with androgenetic alopecia found oral minoxidil 5 mg daily had similar efficacy to topical minoxidil 5% solution applied twice daily after 24 weeks.
- **Safety:** generally considered safe at low doses. Common side effects are hypertrichosis (excess hair growth) and headaches.
- He points readers to Dr. Marjon Vatanchi at Irvine Dermatology as a source for an oral minoxidil prescription.

chunks.heading: What did not work: PRP and PRF
chunks.text:
- Bryan did PRP and PRF, where blood is drawn, the plasma separated, and the plasma reinjected into the scalp.
- He did it diligently for 12 months and saw "nearly no benefit."
- His verdict: it is painful, expensive and time consuming. PRP seems to work for some people but not all.
- He turned to a different treatment method that Blueprint is assessing and may release later in the year if it passes.

chunks.heading: Finasteride, Blueprint products in development, and the future
chunks.text:
- **Finasteride:** Bryan acknowledges many people take oral finasteride with good results. He says he has been able to avoid it and its side-effect risk.
- **Blueprint hair shampoo:** possibly coming. Blueprint has been trialing a formulation he thinks is the best available, pending a completed assessment.
- **Blueprint hair treatment:** also in the works, pending final assessment.
- **Monitoring:** as with any new therapy, watch for side effects.
- **Future therapies:** he is in touch with several companies building novel hair regrowth therapies. He calls them promising but still years away, and imagines hair loss may eventually no longer be something people have to think about.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan details how he reversed receding gums, eroding teeth and bruxism over three years on Blueprint. He explains which dental baselines to measure, his nine-step daily oral care routine, and hygiene tips on sugar, acid, hydration and brushing timing.

chunks.heading: Baseline measurements Bryan asks a dentist to take
chunks.text:
- Bryan says that, as with anything in Blueprint, you need to know your baseline first. He asks his dentist to evaluate three things.
- **Attachment loss:** the loss of supportive tissue around the teeth. Severe poor attachment can lead to tooth loss.
- **Pocket depth:** measured from the top of the gum line to the bottom of the pocket where the gum attaches to the tooth. Healthy gums are 1-3 mm. Three years ago Bryan had several pockets that were 5 mm deep.
- **Plaque index:** the thickness of plaque on the tooth surface. His dentist stained his mouth with a solution that reveals plaque, then assigned numbers to the plaque levels and the parts of the teeth affected.
- He also checks whether the gums bleed. He wants gums that don't bleed easily. His dentist kept poking his gums trying to make them bleed and couldn't.

chunks.heading: Results after three years on Blueprint
chunks.text:
- Bryan started Blueprint with receding gums, eroding teeth and a sugar-heavy diet, and says his teeth caused him a lot of anxiety. His message: caring for your teeth is manageable and reversing damage is possible.
- His dentist reports "you have the gums of a healthy teenager".
- Plaque index of 24.4%, which he calls ideal.
- Gingival and calculus index of 0, the lowest possible and equal to an 18-year-old.
- Attachment loss reduced by 41%.
- He resolved destructive bruxism he had dealt with for 20 years.
- He argues oral health matters beyond teeth: optimal oral care can prevent tooth decay and gum disease, and can lower the risk of heart disease.

chunks.heading: Bryan's nine-step oral care protocol
chunks.text:
Steps 1-6 are done morning and night.
1. **Waterpik:** the first step. A high-pressure water stream removes food, plaque and bacteria from hard-to-reach places.
2. **Floss:** used after the Waterpik has loosened particles. He uses Dr. Tongue's floss because it is thicker and showed a 25%+ increase in plaque removal in studies Blueprint reviewed.
3. **Brush:** an electric brush with soft bristles, which cleans effectively without needless harshness on teeth or gums. He says a manual brush is fine if you prefer it.
4. **Toothpaste:** he currently uses two types, neither containing fluoride.
5. **Tongue scraper:** he calls it "a game changer" and encourages everyone to try it for better oral hygiene.
6. **Mouthwash:** a xylitol mouthwash.
7. **Tea tree oil:** he previously used 2-3 drops in 2 oz of water. It helped his oral health years ago. He stopped recently because his baseline is back to ideal.
8. **Bruxism device:** worn while sleeping. A dentist on Blueprint recommended the SomnoDent bruxism device (SomnoDent Avant). For the first time in 20 years of night grinding, his bruxism stopped. He strongly encourages anyone with bruxism to address it.
9. **Professional cleanings:** at least 2 visits a year, to catch problems early and remove hardened plaque. Even with diligent brushing and flossing, plaque is hard to fully remove at home.

chunks.heading: Daily oral hygiene habits
chunks.text:
- **Reduce sugar:** use alternatives such as trehalose, monk fruit, xylitol and allulose.
- **Limit acidic liquids:** avoid extended exposure to acidic fluids such as coffee and lemon water.
- **Avoid dry mouth:** stay hydrated. Saliva washes away food debris, neutralizes acid and carries ions like calcium that remineralize and strengthen enamel.
- **Wait to brush:** he doesn't brush for 30 minutes after eating, because enamel is temporarily softened.
- **Travel toothbrush:** on days on the go, he carries one and sneaks away to a bathroom during the day for a clean.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan Johnson and the Blueprint clinical team outline seven free at-home fitness tests (push-ups, sit-rise, waist-to-height, grip strength, sit-and-reach, one-leg stand, reaction time) whose results are entered in the Don't Die app to get a biological age. He also points to Blueprint's paid blood panels, microplastics test and Speed of Aging for deeper baselines.

chunks.heading: Free at-home Bioage Fitness tests
chunks.text:
Bryan's Blueprint clinical team designed seven free fitness tests that estimate biological age without lab work. Results are entered in the Don't Die App to produce a biological age.

**How to log results:**
1. Download the Don't Die App.
2. Open the profile and go to "Measurements".
3. Click the + next to "Capabilities".
4. Select the fitness assessment being completed (instructions are in the app).
5. Enter the results to receive a biological age.

chunks.heading: Strength and endurance tests: push-ups and grip strength
chunks.text:
**Continuous push-ups** measure upper body strength and endurance. The goal is as many push-ups as possible without rest.
- Start face down, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, elbows fully extended.
- Lower until the chest touches the floor, body in a straight line from head to heels. Don't round the back.
- Push back up; that is one rep.
- "Without rest" means not holding at the top for 3 seconds.
- Record the total completed with proper form.

**Grip strength** measures hand and forearm strength and correlates with cardiovascular disease risk. Larger numbers are better.
- Use a grip strength dynamometer.
- Stand upright, holding it at your side, and squeeze as hard as possible.
- Do 3 attempts per hand and record the highest reading in lb.

chunks.heading: Mobility and flexibility tests: Sit Rise Test and Sit and Reach
chunks.text:
**Sit Rise Test** assesses flexibility, strength and balance.
- From standing, sit on the floor cross-legged, then rise back to standing, without using hands, knees, forearms or the side of the legs for support.
- Scoring: deduct 1 point for each hand, knee or forearm used going down and up.
- Maximum score is 10; 8 or more is considered ideal.

**Sit and Reach (YMCA)** measures flexibility of the lower back and hamstrings. Reaching further is better.
- Sit with legs straight out in front, feet about 10-12 inches apart.
- Lay one tape measure along the floor and place a second at the 15" mark, crossing the first (~5-6 inch mark) to form a "T" or "+", with zero closest to you. Heels rest on the first tape measure.
- Stack one hand on the other, palms down, and reach forward as far as possible along the measuring line.
- Hold the stretch for 1-2 seconds and measure the distance reached by the fingertips.
- Repeat twice and record the best distance.

chunks.heading: Body composition and balance: waist-to-height ratio and one-leg stand
chunks.text:
**Waist-to-height ratio** assesses body fat distribution, metabolic health and risk. A smaller ratio is better.
- Measure height in cm.
- Measure waist circumference in cm at the narrowest point between the ribs and hips.
- Ratio = waist circumference (cm) / height (cm).

**One-leg stand / balance test** measures balance and lower body strength. Longer is better.
- Stand on one leg with eyes shut, the other leg bent at the knee, lifted and free floating.
- Hold as long as possible without touching the raised leg to the ground, using external support, or touching the other leg.
- Record the time in seconds, and test both legs.

chunks.heading: Reaction time test
chunks.text:
This measures quickness of response to a stimulus. A smaller reaction time is better.
- Download the app "Reaction Time & Reflex Test" and open the game "Lights Out".
- Start a new test and place a thumb or finger on the screen to start the countdown; all 5 lights illuminate.
- Lift the finger or thumb as soon as the lights go out.
- Repeat 5 times and take the best score, which is the lowest number.

chunks.heading: Blueprint Labs for more comprehensive baselines
chunks.text:
For deeper testing than the free fitness assessments, Bryan points to Blueprint Labs, which he says "empowers you with data to take control of your health."
- **Blood panels:** basic tests 60 biomarkers; advanced tests 115. Both are blood and urine tests designed for deep analysis and insights.
- **Microplastics:** described as the world's first at-home microplastics blood test, a finger-prick screen for most common commercial plastics.
- **Speed of Aging:** reports biological age and health for 11 critical organ systems, and how fast or slow aging is occurring.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan reports a 0.48 speed of aging (PACE, DNA methylation), ranking #1 of 5,677 Rejuvenation Olympics competitors. He explains why he built a data-first leaderboard to replace anecdote-driven health advice, argues methodical work can beat genetic gifts, and outlines how to compete with three tests within two years.

chunks.heading: Speed of aging as the core measurement: DNA methylation and PACE
chunks.text:
- Bryan chose "speed of aging" as his headline metric because of how robust and reliable the signal is.
- DNA methylation is a whole-body health marker that integrates thousands of biochemical cues into one measurable signal. The speed of aging algorithm distills it into a single number: an individual's PACE score.
- He contrasts it with narrow markers such as blood glucose, hormones and cholesterol. DNA methylation, and specifically the PACE clock, is "a comprehensive assessment of one's health."
- He says this new biological aging measurement science has begun "nipping at the heels of the best predictors of all-cause mortality" after just a few years.
- The test is an easy at-home finger prick.

chunks.heading: Bryan's result: 0.48 speed of aging
chunks.text:
- Bryan reports the world's slowest speed of aging at 0.48, "breaking the 0.5 barrier" (reported 05.20.2025).
- Meaning: his biological clock ticks at about half speed, so "my birthday now happens every 2 years."
- He ranks #1 out of 5,677 global Rejuvenation Olympics competitors.
- His three-test average is 0.54.

chunks.heading: Why measurement matters: replacing storytelling with data
chunks.text:
- Bryan argues that before Project Blueprint and Don't Die, health influencers and fads were mainly storytelling-based and anecdotal. What was missing was "rigorous science, measurement and data."
- When health decisions run on storytelling, nobody knows what works or who is telling the truth. This leaves people confused and paralyzed.
- This inspired him to make his project the most scientifically rigorous and quantifiable ever, and he says he became "the most biologically measured person in human history."
- His principle: if the goal is Don't Die, you need robust, science-based systems with quantifiable results.

chunks.heading: Blueprint is built on population evidence, not only Bryan's biomarkers
chunks.text:
- Bryan says it is not an accurate criticism that Blueprint is based on his own biomarkers. It is built on population-level scientific evidence.
- The core protocol applies to everyone of all ages.
- Each person's Blueprint can be further customized to individual needs.

chunks.heading: The Rejuvenation Olympics: rejuvenation as a sport
chunks.text:
- Early on, people couldn't categorize him and blurted words like vampire, Patrick Bateman, techbro, biohacker, Prometheus and Dorian Gray.
- He began calling himself a "professional rejuvenation athlete." His reasoning: when LeBron James eats and sleeps well and sets records, he is praised, but when Bryan did the same, "hate rained."
- Framing rejuvenation as a sport gives the practice respect and formality. He created the Rejuvenation Olympics, a leaderboard for people competing on the slowness of their speed of aging.
- He says it sets a level playing field for anyone in health and wellness, since humans love points, status and leaderboards, which any competitive sport needs.
- The leaderboard has also helped the wider health community see which things increase and decrease speed of aging. He promised to post more on this.

chunks.heading: Genetics vs effort
chunks.text:
- Talking with others on the leaderboard, Bryan learned some people naturally (genetically) have a very low speed of aging.
- He met a top-10 competitor with a speed of aging fairly close to his own who does nothing for his health. Bryan says "He is genetically gifted. I am not," while lowering his own speed of aging is a primary focus of his life.
- His takeaway: even without genetic gifts, methodical hard work can meaningfully slow speed of aging and even outperform the genetically gifted.
- He speculates that gene editing might eventually make lowering speed of aging a simple fix, or that it could become a pill.
- Until then, his approach is to understand the science, design evidence-based protocols, and "execute with precision."

chunks.heading: How to compete and get a verified ranking
chunks.text:
1. Get a Blueprint Speed of Aging Test.
2. When registering the test, opt in to the leaderboard.
3. A "verified" ranking requires three tests, all within the previous two years.

- The leaderboard displays your best 3 test results within 2 years. Bryan says this allows experimenting with different interventions and protocols without punishing the learning process.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan ran a 30-day dry sauna experiment and calls sauna one of the most efficacious longevity protocols he has done. He shares his own protocol (200°F, 20 min, daily), a home version (80-100°C, 15-20 min, 3-5x/week), his toxin, microplastic, vascular and fertility results, and safety cautions.

chunks.heading: Dry sauna as a core longevity protocol
chunks.text: Bryan calls dry sauna one of the most efficacious longevity protocols he has done, and now saunas daily. He ran a 30-day test measuring hundreds of markers. He cites long-term studies linking sauna use 4+ times per week to about a 40% lower risk of dying from any cause versus no sauna use. Sauna takes about 20 minutes a day and is available in most gyms. He says it can improve heart, metabolism, skin and brain health.

chunks.heading: What the literature shows (by frequency)
chunks.text:
Bryan summarizes these effects (sessions of at least 19 min for the mortality figures):

| Outcome | 2-3x/week | 4-7x/week |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heart disease risk | -23% | -48% |
| High blood pressure risk (healthy men 42-60) | -17% | -47% |
| Dementia risk | -21% | -48% |
| Systemic inflammation | -17% | -31.5% |
| All-cause mortality | -24% | -40% |
| Heart disease death | -29% | -70% |

- Psychotic disorder risk is 77% lower at 4-7x/week.
- Over 80% of users reported better sleep, and 33% reported less muscle pain.
- Inflammation markers that fall: hsCRP, fibrinogen and white blood cell count.
- Metabolic effects: lower total cholesterol and LDL, a transient drop in triglycerides, and a small rise in HDL (10 sessions of 3 x 15 min).
- In a low-powered study (12 days at 212°F / 100°C, 5 x 10 min, over 4 weeks): muscle mass +1.07%, bone mineral density +7.7%.
- Sweating increases removal of arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury. Sessions of 15-20+ min may help clear stored fat-soluble toxins.

chunks.heading: Why dry sauna works and why alternatives do not
chunks.text:
- Skin heats faster than the core, which inverts the skin-to-core temperature gradient.
- The heart pumps up to 70% more blood, similar to intense aerobic exercise (zone 2).
- The skin makes 0.6-1 liter of sweat per hour.
- Heat tolerance improves, with a lower core body temperature.
- At a core temperature of 102.2°F (39°C), the body releases heat shock proteins that repair misfolded proteins.
- Steam baths, hot tubs and infrared saunas do not replicate this. They do not reach the needed temperatures, induce the same sweating, create the inverted gradient, or redirect blood to the skin.

chunks.heading: Bryan's results after 15 sessions
chunks.text:
**Toxins:** 2,4-D -65%, MEP -100%, MBP -15%, MEHP -100% (undetectable), NAPR -56%, HEMA -56%, perchlorate -100% (undetectable).

**Microplastics:** an 85% drop in ejaculate, with a nearly identical drop in blood microplastics over the same period.

**Vascular function:** a 10-year reduction in vascular age, now that of an elite 18-early 20s.
- Central systolic blood pressure 96 mmHg
- Central pulse pressure 20 mmHg
- Pulse pressure amplification 160%
- SEVR 227%
- Augmentation pressure 1 mmHg
- Augmentation index 3%
- Traditional blood pressure 107/75 mmHg

chunks.heading: Fertility findings and icing the testicles
chunks.text:
- **Without ice**, sauna hurt sperm markers: total motile count -56%, concentration -30%, motility -50%, morphology -48%, count -9%.
- **With ice**, his markers hit an all-time high: total count 600M, concentration 162M, motility 55%, total motile count 330M, normal morphology 10%. He says he has more total and motile sperm than 99.6% of men of any age, including men under 25.
- He does not know whether the gain came from sauna, sauna plus ice, or ice alone. He found no other protocol changes that would explain it.
- Icing method: use a non-toxic reusable ice pack, wear cotton boxers and shorts, place the packs between boxers and shorts, and keep them on for the entire session.
- He argues men should protect fertility even when not trying to conceive. Sperm quality is tightly coupled to testicular function, which governs testosterone, metabolic health and endocrine stability. Declining fertility often signals upstream dysfunction that also drives lower testosterone, higher inflammation and more cardiometabolic risk.

chunks.heading: Bryan's personal sauna protocol
chunks.text:
- Type: dry sauna, 200°F (93°C), humidity very low (5-20%)
- Duration and frequency: 20 min, daily, in the morning after his workout
- Heat protection: ice packs on the testicles, and an ice pack on the head to protect scalp and hair
- Skincare: Blueprint Facial Moisturizer before the sauna; face mask and Blueprint Facial Serum a few times a week after
- Rehydration: 36 oz mineral-supplemented water

chunks.heading: How to sauna at home
chunks.text:
- **Temperature:** 176-212°F (80-100°C). Beginners should aim for the low end, since higher heat can cause headaches and severely dry nose and eyes.
- **Duration and frequency:** 15-20 min, 3-5x a week (his key takeaway range is 3-7x a week).
- **Skin:** apply moisturizer before. Hot dry sauna raises transepidermal water loss and stresses the skin barrier.
- **Head and nose:** wear a sauna hat or a 100% natural cotton towel, or put an ice pack on a towel. Breathe through a towel if needed.
- **Hydration:** never sauna dehydrated. Rehydrate with 16-32 oz (0.5-1 L) of fluid plus electrolytes. To be precise, measure sweat volume and saltiness with a patch (e.g. from Gatorade), since some people have saltier sweat.
- **Toxin avoidance:** wear cotton or bamboo, or go naked. Avoid synthetic towels and heavily treated fabrics. Do not pour water on the rocks. Shower after each session.

chunks.heading: Who should skip sauna, and the fallback
chunks.text:
Skip it if you:
- have serious heart issues or uncontrolled blood pressure
- are pregnant (consult a doctor)
- have an infection, fever or feel unwell
- have a history of seizures
- have respiratory conditions such as asthma or COPD
- have irritated or inflamed skin
- recently consumed alcohol or recreational drugs
- take beta-blockers, stimulants, anticholinergics or diuretics

If you have no sauna, his best alternative is exercise, which raises body heat and gives many of the same cardiovascular benefits. For maximum benefit, do both.

chunks.heading: Summary

It covers 8:30 pm bedtime, light and breath work, a pre-workout stack, 90 min of exercise, daily sauna, red/NIR light, hair and skin care, and a plant-based breakfast. He stresses starting small rather than copying him.

chunks.heading: Bedtime and sleep as the foundation
chunks.text:
- Bryan is in bed by 8:30 pm and wakes naturally around 5 am.

chunks.heading: Wake-up sequence: oral hygiene, light, and breath work

chunks.heading: Exercise: 90 minutes daily

chunks.heading: Sauna, red/NIR light, and shockwave
chunks.text:
**Sauna, 20 min daily:**
- 200°F (93°C)
- Core temperature (measured at the ear) after sauna: 102.4°F (39°C)

chunks.heading: Hair, shower, and skincare

**Hair:**

chunks.heading: Breakfast

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan explains how he falls asleep within 3 minutes nightly, ranking in the 99.4th sleep percentile. The routine centers on a noon final meal, HRV breathing, dim red/amber light, a 60-minute screen-free wind-down, and a consistent 8:30 pm bedtime, with advice to start small.

chunks.heading: Why the final meal is at noon
chunks.text:
Bryan's single most impactful sleep change was moving his final meal to around noon, roughly 8.5 hours before bed.

- When he eats close to bed, his resting heart rate before sleep climbs to 52-56 bpm and he loses roughly 30% of his sleep quality.
- When his heart rate is 39 to 44 bpm, he says his sleep is perfect.
- His reasoning: the body struggles to enter deep sleep while digesting, because it is being asked to do two conflicting things, digest and sleep.
- He says you don't need a noon cutoff. Start by finishing food 2 hours before bed, then move to 3 hours, then 4. Each step shows up in your data the next morning.
- His advice: "Experiment and find what's right for you."

chunks.heading: Results and where to start
chunks.text:
- Bryan says he is asleep within 3 min of his head hitting the pillow, every night.
- His sleep performance ranks in the 99.4th percentile, which he says took 5 years to build systems for.
- His routine changes as his team updates his protocols.
- He says you don't need to copy his routine or overhaul everything. Start small, with turning off screens 60 min before bed.

chunks.heading: HRV therapy and breathing
chunks.text:
- Bryan describes HRV as the variability between heartbeats, with higher HRV reflecting a more resilient nervous system.
- Before bed he does 10 min of 4:6 breathing: in through the nose for 4 seconds, out for 6.
- This activates the parasympathetic nervous system, elevating HRV and calming him for sleep.

chunks.heading: Skin, hair and oral hygiene (done before winding down)
chunks.text:
He does these before the wind-down so that when it's time to sleep he can go straight to bed.

- **Skincare:** Blueprint Gentle Facial Cleanser, SFC Facial Serum and SFC Facial Moisturizer, plus tretinoin nightly.
- **Haircare:** a custom 1 mL topical 5% minoxidil solution applied to the scalp each night. In the morning he applies Blueprint Peptide Hair Serum and takes oral minoxidil.
- **Oral hygiene:** Waterpik, floss, brush teeth, tongue scraper.
- **Bruxism:** he sleeps with a bruxism device (SomnoDent Avant) to prevent teeth grinding.

chunks.heading: Melatonin and lighting
chunks.text:
- **Melatonin:** he takes 300 mcg each night and nothing else for sleep.
- **Lighting:** the only lights in his house are 2 low cost lamps, one amber and one red. Otherwise he cycles his daily routines with the sun.
- His rationale: modern lighting is harsh, and blue light reduces production of the sleep hormone melatonin. Red light helps you unwind.

chunks.heading: 60-min wind-down and "Sleep Bryan"
chunks.text:
- He turns off screens 60 min before bed and enables "Sleep Bryan."
- Sleep Bryan's job is to get his mind and body ready for sleep. When thoughts arise about everything still to be done, he reminds all the other Bryans that "we have all day tomorrow" to take care of these things.
- During this hour he usually hangs out with family, walks and reads.
- He likes a real book in hand 10-20 min before sleep, because it creates separation from devices.
- His tip: set an alarm if you need a reminder to wind down.

chunks.heading: Consistent bedtime
chunks.text:
- Bryan gets into bed at 8:30 pm and is usually asleep within 3 min.
- He says you don't need to go to bed this early, but you should be consistent.
- His rule: choose a time that allows 7-9 hours of sleep, and go to bed within +/- 30 min of that time every night.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan reacts to a study of 16 epigenetic age clocks across many interventions and maps the results to his own protocol. He explains why he stopped rapamycin, keeps metformin, avoids grains, trusts the DunedinPACE clock, and why single clocks and rodent data are unreliable proxies for human longevity.

chunks.heading: Study design: 16 epigenetic clocks used to rank interventions
chunks.text:
Bryan summarizes a December 2024 study that scored interventions against 16 epigenetic age clocks.

- **Slowed biological aging:** anti-TNF therapy, metformin, ketamine, AC11 supplement, TruLacta, gastric bypass, smoking cessation, kidney transplant, HBOT (large average effect, not statistically significant), vegan diet, green Mediterranean diet, Mediterranean diet, low-fat and low-carb diets.
- **Accelerated biological aging:** rapamycin, senolytics, buckwheat extract, follistatin gene therapy, kidney dialysis.
- His main takeaway: "continuous measurement and optimization for actual biomarkers and performance indicators automatically consolidates the interventions that best slow down epigenetic biological age." Many findings matched what his protocol already did.

chunks.heading: Rapamycin: why he stopped
chunks.text:
- In September 2024 he stopped rapamycin because his lab results showed metabolic side effects: higher cholesterol, blood sugar and resting heart rate.
- The study showed rapamycin raised biological age on 2 clocks and did nothing on the rest.
- Rapamycin is consistently the strongest drug at extending mouse lifespan in gold-standard ITP studies. Bryan says this "puts to question the validity of rodent data in predicting longevity interventions in humans."

chunks.heading: Metformin and anti-TNF: what he keeps and what it signals
chunks.text:
- He continues taking metformin.
- In the study, 5 of 16 clocks showed a significant reduction or slowdown in biological age, and no clock showed the opposite.
- Counterweights he considers outweighed:
  - Mouse ITP studies failed to show lifespan extension.
  - Claims that it blunts muscle growth. He says he is top 0.1% of his age group for muscle volume.
- Supporting evidence he cites: aging clocks in non-human primates (particularly in the brain) and lower cancer incidence in retrospective population studies.
- Anti-TNF therapy lowered biological age across most clocks. He reads this as showing the importance of "inflammaging" in driving aging.

chunks.heading: Diet: green Mediterranean, grain-free, and the buckwheat result
chunks.text:
- A green Mediterranean diet did best, slowing aging on 10 of 16 clocks. He says it is the closest to his Blueprint diet.
- He stays grain-free. Buckwheat extract produced a slight but significant acceleration in aging clocks, which he takes as validation.
- His explanation for buckwheat:
  - It is rich in B vitamins, which drive the methylation cycle.
  - That raises genome-wide methylation, as seen in a large elderly cohort study, potentially accelerating age-related epigenetic change.
  - Long-term B9 (folate) supplementation raised cancer incidence and all-cause mortality, with the effect correlated to blood folate concentration.
- Organ-system clocks and DNAm proxies reproduced known diet effects, for example vegan and Mediterranean diets reducing inflammation and low-carb reducing HbA1c.

chunks.heading: Follistatin gene therapy: his personal data
chunks.text:
- The study found follistatin gene therapy increased biological age, driven mainly by the PACE clock.
- Bryan received the therapy from Minicircle, and it raised his circulating follistatin.
- After the therapy, his PACE score dropped from 0.70 to 0.64. He calls this associative, not proof of causation, but reassuring that it had no undesired effect on his biological age.
- He is investigating whether the studied cohort was healthy or disease-specific, since that changes how the result should be read.
- Minicircle's preprint found no PACE change. It did find a mild reduction in Extrinsic Epigenetic Age, strongly correlated with T and B immune cells.

chunks.heading: Which aging clocks he trusts and how he tracks himself
chunks.text:
- He continuously tracks his epigenetic age with DunedinPACE (PACE), which he calls superior in reliability and sensitivity, especially for shifts in healthy people.
- He says he is, as far as he knows, "the most epigenetic-measured person in the world."
- In the study's reliability comparison, DunedinPACE always agreed with the majority of other clocks or was the only one to detect a change.
- Why healthy-cohort sensitivity matters:
  - Disease treatment gives larger, easier-to-detect improvements.
  - True longevity interventions should lower biological age in healthy people too, since they address aging itself.
- Three clocks detected effects in healthy cohorts, including DunedinPACE. GrimAge (mortality-predicting) worked in both healthy and disease contexts.
- He describes the newest "Gen X" (explainable) clocks as linking aging to specific organs (organ-system clocks) and biomarkers (DNAm proxies), much as conventional studies identify a drug's mechanism.

chunks.heading: Limits of aging clocks
chunks.text:
- Clocks are a surrogate endpoint for lifespan. Waiting on mortality data alone "would delay the field by several decades."
- Clocks were not designed to predict therapy effects, so they can isolate negative effects while missing beneficial ones.
- He argues single-clock approaches and animal data are unreliable for judging human longevity outcomes, which is why multiple clocks and real biomarkers are needed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan Johnson lists 14 steps he took after testing his home and finding toxins everywhere: remove shoes, monitor and filter air, clean water, avoid plastics, non-stick pans and gas stoves, and control light and noise for sleep. Many fixes are quick or free, and he stresses patience since it took him 5 years.

chunks.heading: Shoes off and indoor air quality
chunks.text:
- Bryan takes his shoes off at the door. Shoes carry in lead, asbestos, pesticides, feces, metals and microplastics, which are then far more likely to get into the body.
- He runs 2 monitors. One tracks CO2, PM1 (ultrafine particles that can enter the bloodstream), PM2.5 (reaches deep into the lungs) and PM10 (coarse dust). The other shows indoor and outdoor AQI.
- The monitors show him whether his air purifiers and HVAC filter are working.
- Quick win: a portable HEPA air purifier in the bedroom, running while he sleeps.

chunks.heading: HVAC filter and safety sensors
chunks.text:
- He treats the HVAC system as the first line of defense for air quality. He upgrades the filter and cleans it regularly.
- MERV rates an air filter's particle capture. A MERV 8 filter captures ~30% of PM2.5.
- He goes as high as the system is rated and no higher, because exceeding the rating can cause problems. His system handles MERV 13.
- With an air monitor, the effect of a better filter shows up within minutes.
- Smoke alarms: 3 in 5 home-fire deaths involve dead or missing alarms. He says to press the test button once a month.
- He recommends a carbon monoxide detector (CO kills 400 Americans a year).
- He recommends a radon test. Radon is an invisible, odorless gas from the earth and the second-most prominent cause of lung cancer after smoking.

chunks.heading: Water: reverse osmosis
chunks.text:
- Tap water can contain heavy metals, PFAS, microplastics, pesticides, volatile organic compounds and pharmaceutical residues.
- Bryan uses a reverse osmosis system. Tap water has over 300 mg/L of dissolved solids; with RO it drops to 25 mg/L.
- He says the RO system should include a remineralization step for electrolyte balance.
- He cleans or replaces filters every few months, or as the filtration company recommends.

chunks.heading: Plastics, cookware and the stove
chunks.text:
- He has spent months removing plastics from his house and still occasionally finds more.
- Swaps: wooden chopping boards, stainless steel utensils, glass storage containers.
- Non-stick pans contain PFAS ("forever chemicals"), which can last up to decades in the body. He uses stainless steel or cast iron instead.
- Gas stoves are linked to increased childhood asthma risk. Even 1 gas burner spikes nitrogen dioxide and fine particles.
- Options: replace with an induction stove, use a ducted vent hood, or cook on the stove less often.

chunks.heading: Cleaning products and carpets
chunks.text:
- Scented sprays and air fresheners release volatile organic compounds, which react with oxygen to form formaldehyde, a known carcinogen.
- His rules for cleaning products:
  - Avoid phthalates, ammonia, quat, chlorine bleach and formaldehyde.
  - Look for EPA Safer Choice, EWG Verified or Green Seal certifications.
  - Avoid scented sprays and air fresheners.
  - Open the windows when cleaning.
- Carpet holds 10x the dust, allergens and microbes of hard floors. With carpet, he says to use a HEPA vacuum 2x a week.
- A good HEPA filter removes 99.97% of microplastic particles.

chunks.heading: UV from windows
chunks.text:
- Non-tinted glass lets ~37-73% of UVA through. UVA contributes to skin aging and skin cancer risk.
- Bryan has window film that filters 99% of UVA and UVB.
- He is not anti-sun; he wants controlled exposure, and all-day sun through windows can exceed it.
- Cheaper alternatives: close blinds during high-UV hours (10am-4pm) or move to a room without direct sun.
- His principle: "Be sun smart in your home like you would be outside."

chunks.heading: Evening and bedroom environment for sleep
chunks.text:
- Red light: blue light lowers melatonin and makes falling asleep harder. Bryan uses a ~$30 red lamp in the evening, dim, ~2 hours before bed.
- Darkness: even 10 lux (very dim street lighting) can halve melatonin production and fragment sleep. In his testing, a blacked-out bedroom substantially improves sleep quality. Options are blackout blinds or curtains, or an eyemask.
- Noise: when he lived next to a busy road, a noise machine smoothed out the traffic noise and improved his sleep quality.
- He suggests white noise (TV static), brown noise (rumbling thunder) or pink noise (wind), and says pink is best because it is less high-pitched than white.
- He advises measuring your sleep to see whether it works for you.

chunks.heading: Mindset on home toxins
chunks.text:
- Bryan says to avoid feeling anxious about toxins: "They are everywhere… but you can remove the big ones."
- He says to be patient. It took him 5 years to improve his home environment, and he advises baby steps.
- Some steps are quick and free, such as shoes off at the door and closing blinds at peak UV.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bryan explains his decision to end almost five years of rapamycin experimentation. Across weekly, biweekly and alternating protocols, the side effects (infections, lipid and glucose changes, higher resting heart rate) outweighed the longevity benefits, and new epigenetic clock data added to the concern.

chunks.heading: Why Bryan stopped rapamycin
chunks.text:
On September 28th, Bryan decided to stop rapamycin, ending almost 5 years of experimentation with the molecule for its longevity potential. He and his team concluded that "the benefits of lifelong dosing of Rapamycin do not justify the hefty side-effects."

- Despite the immense potential seen in pre-clinical trials, the trade-off did not hold up in his own data.
- He stresses that longevity research on experimental compounds keeps evolving. He and his team watch both the research and his biomarkers constantly.

chunks.heading: Protocols Bryan tested
chunks.text:
Over almost 5 years he tried several dosing schedules to optimize rejuvenation and limit side effects:

- Weekly dosing at 5 mg, 6 mg and 10 mg
- Biweekly dosing at 13 mg
- Alternating weekly dosing at 6 mg and 13 mg

Changing the dose or schedule did not remove the side effects.

chunks.heading: Side effects that drove the decision
chunks.text:
- Intermittent skin and soft tissue infections
- Lipid abnormalities
- Glucose elevations
- Increased resting heart rate

No other underlying cause was identified. The team suspected rapamycin, and because dosage adjustments had no effect, they discontinued it entirely rather than keep tuning the dose.

chunks.heading: Research concerns Bryan cites on metabolism
chunks.text:
- Preclinical and clinical research indicates prolonged rapamycin use can disrupt lipid metabolism and lipid profiles.
- It can induce insulin and glucose intolerance.
- It has been linked to pancreatic beta-cell toxicity.

These findings match the lipid and glucose changes he saw in his own biomarkers.

chunks.heading: Cancer and immune surveillance concern
chunks.text:
- Bryan acknowledges anecdotal evidence that rapamycin slows tumor growth.
- He points to research showing rapamycin inhibits natural killer cells, which raises concerns about anti-cancer immune surveillance and cancer risk over the longer run.

chunks.heading: Epigenetic clock evidence
chunks.text:
- On October 25th, a new pre-print indicated rapamycin was one of a handful of supposed longevity interventions that caused an increase or acceleration of aging in humans across 16 epigenetic aging clocks.
- Bryan notes this evaluation is the first of its kind. Most longevity interventions have been tested against only one or two aging clocks, which leads to "invisible biases and potential intended 'cherry picking' of favorable clocks."
- Testing across many clocks is a stronger check on whether an intervention truly slows aging.

chunks.heading: Measuring all 70+ organs and reversing biological age (Project Blueprint)
chunks.text:
- Project Blueprint aims to measure all 70+ organs and then maximally reverse the quantified biological age of each.
- As of October 2021, over 15 organs were measured and Bryan had scored 507 age reversal points.
- His chronological age was 44 and his measured biological age was 36.
- He calls Blueprint "a stock ticker of sorts" that reveals the status of anti-aging science through tracking biological versus chronological age (an N=1 for now).
- Aging escape velocity: reversing measured biological age by 1.01 years for every year that passes would be evidence that life expectancy increases faster than time passes.
- On a magic pill, he says that for the foreseeable future, "achieving and maintaining peak wellness is just going to be a lot of really hard work."
- Blueprint is not Quantified Self or Life Optimization. He frames it as "an exploration into the future of being human."

chunks.heading: Evidence standards and how interventions are chosen
chunks.text:
- For every measurement and intervention, the team finds literature that establishes an age reference range.
- They then identify gold-standard randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence to reverse that age marker, and begin trialing interventions.
- They partner with local practitioners and custom compounded pharmacies, and iterate on novel approaches.
- Rules he states: "we never act on anecdotes," never do something because others do it, and use evidence-based medicine only.
- He "trusts his gut" only through its data (biomarkers), not through subjective emotional states.
- The team publicly journals its efforts monthly, like Lewis & Clark and Shackleton chronicled expeditions.
- He says the system matters more than the specific diet: Blueprint is "a time-consuming, tedious, costly, experimental evidence-based process to create systems that automatically self improve over time." The goal is for it to become transferable so anyone can find the best diet for their body.

chunks.heading: Firing "Evening Bryan" and the Autonomous Self
chunks.text:
- The project began when he fired "Evening Bryan" from authority over what and how much to eat: no late-night binges, no second servings, no "just-this-once" rationalizations.

- This gives the heart, liver, kidneys and other organs an independent voice whose authority surpasses his conscious mind. He calls this his Autonomous Self.
- He describes demoting his conscious mind as one of the most positive developments of his life.
- Broader aim: free people from daily health management so they can focus on building the future. He cites A.N. Whitehead: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking of them."
